articles.title: The techlash has gone Hollywood
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 147, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, I missed you all, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
The techlash has gone Hollywood
Plus, in this week’s Installer: Amazon’s new tablet, a new book on the AI industry, Star Wars racing, and more.
I’m back from parental leave! Part time, anyway. Thanks to everyone who sent well wishes and tips for managing three kids. I need ’em all. This week, I’ve been reading about McMansions and data centers and sports cardsand ICANN, trying to run my life on the Dell XPS Googlebook, testing a new and very purple Kindle, reinventing my whole note-taking system now that Google Docs can handle Markdown files, listening to episode after episode of No Such Thing as a Fish,and watching all of Shrinkingbetween the hours of 1 and 5AM while feeding a baby.
I also have for you the new Facebook movie, a tech-related procedural, a couple of great new gadgets, the Star Wars game that is going to destroy my productivity, a terrific book about the AI industry, and much more. Let’s do this.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What have you been watching / reading / playing / listening to / putting in the air fryer this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- The Social Reckoning. My hopes were not super high for this movie, and the reaction so far suggests it’s good but a far cry from The Social Network. (Which I just watched recently, and absolutely still rips.) Still, Aaron Sorkin and Jeremy Strong will end up in the annals of Big Tech Movies, and I will not be missing this one.
- The Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. For the first time ever, Amazon decided — and I know this might sound far-fetched — to just build an awesome tablet. And it seems it may have! There’s lots of testing to do, and I’m particularly curious about this high-end model with the fancy screen, but I’m hopeful this is the “iPad but cheaper” we’ve been waiting for. For years.
- The AGI Chronicles. However bizarre you think the AI industry is, I promise Kevin Roose’s book will convince you it’s even more so. Roose has been deep inside the AI labs for the last few years, and I think came out with the most important story in AI: how a few executives, and the relationships between them, somehow came to determine the future of everything.
- Star Wars: Galactic Racer. It’s a super high-fidelity Star Wars racing game in which you (eventually) get to pilot a podracer. That’s all I needed to hear! Oh, and if you’re a Prime subscriber, you can play it for free on Amazon’s Luna service.
- Cupertino. The folks who made The Good Wife made a show about technology, and it is exactly what you think it is. I kind of love it! What I’ve seen so far is pretty thoughtful about some complicated real-life legal stuff in tech and AI, and the procedural setup is frankly a nice break from all these miniseries and four-hour docs.
- The Surface Laptop Ultra. Microsoft revealed all the details of its most impressive laptop, and while it’s expensive ($2,600!), it also looks and sounds fantastic. Microsoft is pushing the device’s AI capabilities, but this also looks like the uncompromising MacBook Pro competition a lot of Windows users might want.
- Gears of War: E-Day. When it comes to raw, brutal combat, Gears doesn’t miss very often. This one also seems to deliver on story and exploration, which aren’t always the series’ strong points; a lot of people have been waiting for the origin-story title, and I’m thrilled the game pulls it off.
- Blockers. Michael Lewis tells the story of Elon Musk and DOGE, and in particular of the government employees who tried to stop them from running roughshod over the federal government. I really enjoyed The Fifth Risk, Lewis’ last book about the government, and I expect to like this one too.
One thing about parental leave is that it involves a lot of time with one hand free. Over the last seven weeks I’ve spent dozens, maybe hundreds of hours on the couch while a tiny potato of a baby sleeps or cries or farts on top of me. So what did I do with all that time? Goofed around on my phone, mostly. Too much Reddit, too much TikTok, mercifully at least a little reading and crosswording.
I also redid my entire homescreen, because of course I did, and I figured I’d share. Here’s my current setup:
The phone: iPhone 17. I have no desire to upgrade to the 18… but I find myself hopelessly lusting after a Duo. I must not give in.
The wallpaper: Black. I am on an endless quest to make my phone less interesting to look at, and this helps. It also helps make my phone a little less blaring when I’m looking at it in the dark, which I do a lot these days.
The apps: Unread, Instapaper, Google Maps, Capacities, Daygame, Flora, Phone, Pocket Casts, Spotify, Camera, Prism, Mimestream, Arc.
A few things I want to mention here:
- The widgets at the top are Calendars and Acme Weather. Acme is a fabulous weather app, and I love the hourly widget; Calendars is, like, fine. I switch between it and Fantastical all the time. I don’t think I like any calendar app.
- The only truly new things on my homescreen are Flora and Prism. Flora is a journaling app currently in TestFlight for Apple devices, and it is fabulous. It’s simple and straightforward, but also pulls in workout data, photos, and more to give a really cool snapshot of your day. Prism is a note-taking app that is as fast as texting yourself but with many more organizational powers. I have spent forever looking for a quick, transient way to jot stuff down and organize it later; Prism might be it.
- In case you’re following my endless search for notes apps: I’m back on Capacities, which finally clicked for me. It is a project to get the app fully customized, but it turns out to work exactly like my brain does.
- I switched from Readwise Reader to Instapaper because I recently bought a Kobo, and Instapaper is so nicely integrated into the device. I like the whole setup, but also the Boox Palma 3 is coming, so my reading universe might be in for yet another overhaul soon.
- Daygame, in the middle there, is a thing I built for myself to manage all the daily games I play — it’s just a page full of links to games, which open in various apps and tabs. I might try and spruce it up and share it more widely. Send games I should include!
Before I forget, a few more recommendations from my parental leave:
- Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die. Maybe the strangest movie I watched over the last couple of months, and certainly the one that made me think the most about tech and AI and the future we’re heading toward.
- Tuner. A movie about a piano tuner who falls into a world of safecracking. Nothing I say about this movie will make it sound compelling, but I promise: It’s great.
- Furious. One of the most intense, propulsive crime shows I’ve seen in forever. Could barely put it down.
- Footnotes. A really cool (Apple-only) journaling and notes app, with emphasis on taking pictures and video right next to your notes. One of the most uniquely designed mobile apps I’ve ever used.
- Podcast Shuffle. I had no idea I needed this app until I tried it. You just press a button, and it randomly plays an episode from whatever podcast or podcasts you’ve selected. I use it for falling asleep, I use it for long drives, I love not having to scroll just to get something playing.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Playing StarCraft II since the announcement of a new StarCraft in 2030. Just learned that macOS will drop support of Rosetta 2 in 2028 so no more StarCraft for Mac.” — Christian
“I’m going on a 13-hour road trip, once again guided solely by an old-school Garmin dashboard-mounted GPS. (DriveSmart series; I forget what size.) I like that it’s a single-purpose device with no ads, no subscriptions, and that continues to get map updates.” — sringsmuth
“The recent Hyperfixed podcast episode about the microwave popcorn button is one of the Verge-iest non Verge podcasts I’ve heard in a long time. A BUTTON IS A PROMISE.” — MrEnthusiasm
“I recently finished playing Wolverine on PS5, and I’m blown away by its incredible story and graphics. Insomniac delivered on that unspoken promise of slashing and dashing through bad guys — it feels like a whole new level for the character and for fans of Wolverine.” — Josue
“Just saw Other Mommy. It’s like a fun amusement park ride in the form of a campy horror film.” — Kevin
“I’m building a shed. The tech angle is learning new things using YouTube, online library books, and some AI reviews of local building code pdfs to check if I missed anything. I’m probably doing it all wrong, but that’s what the fire pit is for.” — Tim
“I have fallen headfirst into retro gaming on a Nintendo 3DS XL. The catalog of DS & 3DS games is absolutely massive. Running on native, easily reparable hardware, it’s hard to beat in terms of performance and cost. Ok…back to Picross 3D.” — Jacob
“The Ezra Klein interview with the ex-OpenAI guy and the Jon Stewart interview with the other ex-OpenAI guy.” — Chung
“I have been listening to World War II by Tom Hanks from the History Channel.” — Michael
Signing off
You might already know about the HTX Studio YouTube channel, but if you don’t, trust me, you need to check it out. It’s a team of makers and creators from China who are making some of the most innovative tech videos I’ve seen in years. I have watched their video about AirDesk approximately 25 times, and I want that desk more every single time I see it. The channel is a bit over a year old, and I have yet to find an HTX video that isn’t worth the time — even the one about the cow.
See you next week!

articles.title: El caso de Daniel Sancho tendrá su 'true crime' en Netflix: primeras imágenes oficiales
articles.text:
El caso de Daniel Sancho sigue dando que hablar y va a dar el salto hacia el mundo de las ficciones televisivas. Netflix está preparando un true crime basado en los eventos que derivaron en la detención del español, hijo del actor Rodolfo Sancho, tras el homicidio y el descuartizamiento del médico colombiano Edwin Arrieta en Tailandia, ocurrido en 2023.
La plataforma de streaming ha lanzado las primeras imágenes de la miniserie sobre el caso de Daniel Sancho y ha confirmado a su protagonista. El encargado del rol principal es Martiño Rivas (El internado/Las chicas del cable), a quien ya se ha podido ver caracterizado como Sancho para esta producción.
Los detalles sobre la serie del caso de Daniel Sancho son todavía escasos. Se ha confirmado que el rodaje se llevará a cabo tanto en España como en Tailandia. Asimismo, desde Netflix informaron que la producción de este proyecto estará a cargo de Bambú Producciones, la empresa que lidera Ramón Campos.
Esta no es la primera vez que Campos y Netflix unen sus caminos. En el pasado han trabajado juntos en Las chicas del cable, El caso Asunta, Valle salvaje y Manual para señoritas.
Un dato curioso es que el true crime del caso de Daniel Sancho todavía no tiene título oficial, ni tampoco fecha de estreno. No obstante, se esperan más novedades en los próximos meses. Las primeras imágenes oficiales de la miniserie muestran a Rivas llevando una larga melena como la de Sancho, replicando la imagen viral de su arresto con las manos cubiertas para que no se vean las esposas.
Netflix prepara una miniserie del caso de Daniel Sancho
Por supuesto que Netflix no es la primera en abordar el caso de Daniel Sancho en producciones audiovisuales. En 2024, por ejemplo, HBO Max lanzó un documental basado en el episodio que derivó en la detención y la condena del protagonista. Pero la nueva producción apunta a reconstruir todo lo sucedido desde la óptica de la ficción, lo cual seguramente ayudará a mantener (y tal vez redoblar) la discusión de los hechos en el ámbito popular.
El asesinato de Edwin Arrieta conmocionó a toda España y Colombia en el verano de 2023, cuando su cuerpo apareció descuartizado en Tailandia. Desde entonces, Daniel Sancho y su defensa trataron de conseguir la sentencia más favorable posible, pues sobre la mesa se encontraba incluso la pena de muerte. Al final, el español fue sentenciado a cadena perpetua, condena que está cumpliendo en una prisión del país asiático.
Días atrás, la defensa del susodicho presentó una petición ante el Tribunal Supremo tailandés para que anule el fallo que ratificó su condena. Por lo pronto, Daniel Sancho no puede solicitar el traslado a una cárcel española, pues primero debe cumplir al menos 8 años del castigo en Tailandia.

articles.title: Small businesses that adopt AI are more optimistic about growth, revenue, and employment
articles.text:
Small businesses that adopt AI are more optimistic about growth, revenue, and employment
AI is likely helping to unlock more revenue
- SMBs using AI are more likely to expect a positive impact on employment
- AI could be helping them to overcome constraints and unlock more revenue
- Expectations vs. reality gap shows only 31% have increased sales so far
A new study by the NY Federal Reserve Bank has revealed SMBs who actually adopt AI feel far more optimistic about hiring and revenue growth than non-adopters, and the data comes from a near 50:50 split, because nearly half (46%) of US SMBs already use AI, it found.
AI adopters reportedly recorded a 33 percentage point net expectation of higher employment in the next year compared with 15 percentage points for non-adopters, which is more than double.
But with only one in two (51%) adopters having actually integrated AI into their business processes either partially or fully, many are likely still just experimenting with the tech and not embedded it into actual use cases.
Positivity about AI is actually strongest among AI adopters
On the jobs front, while initial concerns largely centered around AI replacing human workers, three in four (77%) of the surveyed businesses actually reported no change in their current labor costs due to AI, indicating that AI is largely assisting existing workers rather than outright replacing them.
But that's not to say that finances are set to stay flat – it's actually a much more positive story. Adopters are the most likely to expect healthy revenue growth, and the businesses that are struggling the most financially could be among the most optimistic.
Still, expectations and reality are totally different metrics, and fewer than one in three (31%) have actually reported increased sales due to using AI.
"In other words, it seems unlikely that the association between AI use and positive revenue expectations is spurious," the report concludes.

articles.title: The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
articles.text:
I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck.
The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
Tiny pickup trucks might just become a thing in the US if the California-based startup Telo has its way.
The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
Tiny pickup trucks might just become a thing in the US if the California-based startup Telo has its way.
The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.
It has a nearly cab-over design, meaning that front-seat passengers sit almost directly over the front axle. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights or roll silently past.
The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.
Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago.
People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights
Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds. The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees.
Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area. The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.
“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters. “I mean, they’re fun to be up super high and look out and feel like you’re dominating the world, but they’re killing an extra, roughly, 5,000 people per year, so do we want to just give them a pass for that?”
How Telo was born
Marks and North both live and work in the San Francisco Bay Area with their families, and both own pickup trucks: Marks because he has a 150lb three-legged dog he shuttles back and forth to the office every day, and North because he has a passion for the outdoors. Large pickup trucks can be useful, but they’re far from suitable for city life. That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022.
Marks previously worked on automotive safety and validation at National Instruments, while North is a former battery engineer at Tesla, founder of Mission Motors (one of the first electric motorcycle companies to break the land speed record for an electric motorcycle), and cofounder of Recargo, which developed EV charging app PlugShare. Behar is the founder of fuseproject, an industrial design and brand development firm. Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted. It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks.
“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”
— Telo cofounder Forrest North
Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles. Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck. Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup. Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete. They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck. The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck.
“It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said. “The only thing they can do now is be big.” Telo aims to change the conversation about what electric transportation in urban centers can look like.
Battery, range, and layout
For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range. At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range. The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture. The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco.
Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house. Each cell is individually fused so that a single failure won’t trigger a cascade across the pack. According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management. The passive thermal management system operates while the vehicle is parked, maintaining cooler temperatures even in direct sunlight, while active liquid cooling engages only when the vehicle is running. Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago.
For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range
I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing. From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest. With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed.
To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed. It’s accessible from either side and is large enough for a pair of roll-aboard carry-on suitcases to slide in endwise. Marks said that while they knew the front of the MT1 would be difficult to engineer, adding the monster tunnel created a tough engineering challenge because it sits exactly where the battery pack connects.
The interior is still being finalized, but Marks said that it will get two 13-inch digital displays that will support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. The steering wheel also has small scroll wheels, but most features will be controlled through the screen interface.
How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks
Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US. But making that actually happen is far more complicated because kei vehicles don’t meet US crash safety regulations.
Marks claimed that Telo has solved this problem with a completely new front end and an innovative front hinge pillar that took nearly four years to develop and hundreds of thousands of hours of simulated crashes to verify. In the Telo, the redesigned hinge pillar does the structural job of a conventional one while also carrying the strut mount, the cross-car beam, and the dash — consolidating several separate parts into one. This allowed the company to cut the front-end part count roughly in half, Marks said.
“We pretty much threw all [the conventional crash architecture] away and had to start from scratch,” Marks said. The company’s team includes Tesla’s former head of crash safety, brought on to help tackle the new front end and completely reengineer it.
“We have effectively six crash [paths], two bumper beams and two shock structures, a completely different architecture of a hinge pillar, a completely different architecture of a torque box to distribute the energy appropriately to the various parts of the car and save that occupant compartment as much as possible,” he said, comparing the crash innovations to those in a Smartcar. “Would any other automaker say we’re going to bet the world on being able to rethink crash?”
The company’s team includes Tesla’s former head of crash safety
AI tools have made the virtual crash-testing process much more affordable for startups, and Telo recently locked in its body in white, the sheet metal shell made up of the major structural pieces of the truck (think of it like a skeleton of a vehicle). It’s currently being built by US supplier Schwab Industries in Michigan.
Marks said Telo uses AI to run virtual crash tests around the clock, averaging roughly one test per hour. The next phase of crash testing will include cutting the body in white apart for what Marks called a “quasi-static validation,” and full crash testing (slamming the vehicle and its various parts into a wall to validate the virtual testing the company has done) will start next year before Telo starts customer deliveries.
“I think it’s one of the most exciting times to start a hardware company,” North said. “It’s always been like, hardware is hard. That’s always been the cliché, and I wouldn’t say hardware is easy, but I would say it’s gotten so much easier because of software and AI.”
Pricing, delivery, and other features
The Telo MT1 will come in single-motor (rear-wheel drive) and dual-motor (all-wheel drive) layouts and offer add-ons like a solar-capable tonneau cover or camping shell. Reservations are open now for a refundable $152, and the base vehicle starts at $41,520. Marks said the company isn’t really worried about larger competitors like Ford’s upcoming midsized electric truck or Slate’s bare-bones EV because he sees their market entry as proof that a viable market exists for small electric pickup trucks.
North argued that Telo is also in a better position than either Slate or Ford right now because the company has fewer parts moving in and out of the country; it’s assembling its own battery packs and building the body in white stateside, making it largely exempt from the Trump administration’s tariffs. “The pack is the most expensive part of the vehicle build and the heart and soul of the vehicle,” Marks said, “so we had to keep it in-house.”
Marks said he’s been surprised by the volume of reservations: just over 14,000, with 70 percent of reservation-holders configuring AWD versions with the longer-range battery pack. He also noted that around 20 percent are first-time car buyers.
Telo is aiming for profitability at around 5,000 vehicles within roughly 24 months of deliveries. The company plans to get vehicles into customers’ hands sometime in 2027, depending on the validation timelines, but the MT1 still has to go through EPA and California air quality certification. Most reservations have come from places like LA, New York, the Bay Area, Seattle, Dallas, Washington, DC, Miami, and Denver, with almost everyone opting for the larger battery pack, regardless of drive configuration.
Marks pointed to Tesla as the trailblazer of EVs’ first real wave, proving electric cars could be fast, fun, and sporty. However, he believes the industry ultimately missed the chance to fully exploit their potential. Telo is tackling the problem by rethinking vehicle architecture from the ground up, returning to a “one-box” design made possible by eliminating wasted space.
Ultimately, Telo’s focus comes down to purpose, according to Marks: “What does electric enable for the experience of the user, and what value does that bring?”
While history has shown that the market isn’t kind to EV startups, in a world where giant American trucks increasingly barely fit in an average parking spot, the Telo MT1 and its creators are aiming to offer a capable electric pickup built for today’s cramped cities in the hope that Americans can get behind smaller and more capable electric vehicles.

articles.title: Open source : le code vient d’Europe, mais les décisions se prennent ailleurs
articles.text:
Selon la Linux Foundation, 94% des organisations européennes jugent la souveraineté numérique importante, mais seules 37% participent à la gouvernance des projets open source dont elles dépendent.
Bruxelles compte mobiliser 2 milliards d'euros sur sept ans (public et privé) pour réduire sa dépendance aux fournisseurs non européens. Selon le rapport 2026, présenté le 7 octobre à l'Open Source Summit Europe, l'argent ne suffira pas si les Européens ne siègent pas là où les projets se décident.
59% envoient du code, 37% siègent là où le projet se décide
L'enquête a réuni 367 organisations de juin à août, recrutées notamment via les réseaux de la Linux Foundation. Côté code, les Européens signent près de 40% des contributions à des projets comme Kubernetes ou OpenStack, et 59% des organisations renvoient leurs correctifs au projet d'origine (la contribution "upstream"). Mais la gouvernance, c'est-à-dire les comités qui fixent la feuille de route et les règles, ne concerne que 37% d'entre elles.
Lancée en décembre 2025 autour du Model Context Protocol (un standard qui relie les agents IA à des outils), l'Agentic AI Foundation compte huit membres platine fondateurs, tous américains : AWS, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft et OpenAI. SUSE, SAP et Ericsson, seuls Européens, sont aux niveaux or et argent. À noter que la Linux Foundation héberge elle-même cette fondation. Pour Thierry Carrez, directeur général de Linux Foundation Europe, utiliser l'open source "ne donne pas un contrôle effectif sur la technologie".
48% des organisations maintiennent un "fork", une copie privée d'un logiciel qu'il faut ensuite corriger seul. Celles qui le font y passent en général 311 heures par cycle de publication, pour 9,5 forks, et 28% d'entre elles ne savent pas chiffrer ce temps. Les organisations dotées d'une gouvernance avancée déclarent des bénéfices égaux à 4,6 fois leurs coûts, contre 3,6 fois sans gouvernance formelle. Ce sont des estimations des répondants (87 organisations), et le rapport précise qu'elles ne prouvent pas que la gouvernance explique cet écart.
Les outils d'IA saturent les mainteneurs, et la conformité approche
La sécurité et la vie privée arrivent en tête des raisons de la souveraineté (71%). Or les mainteneurs, ceux qui entretiennent ces projets, croulent sous les rapports de bugs et les correctifs générés par IA. Greg Kroah-Hartman, développeur du noyau Linux, indique que le nombre de CVE (les identifiants publics de failles) publiés pour le noyau est passé de 55 à 230 par semaine depuis l'arrivée de ces outils. Une partie correspond à de vrais bugs, parfois anciens. Mais lors de tests avec des étudiants de la Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, près de la moitié des modifications produites par les IA étaient incorrectes. Les mainteneurs du noyau exigent donc que l'auteur prouve que son changement fonctionne.
Le Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), qui impose des exigences de sécurité aux produits numériques vendus dans l'UE, ajoute en plus un peu de pression. Depuis le 11 septembre, les fabricants doivent signaler toute faille activement exploitée et tout incident grave dès qu’ils en ont connaissance : alerte sous 24 heures, puis notification sous 72 heures. Le reste du texte s’applique fin 2027. Or 66% des personnes interrogées dans une autre étude de la Linux Foundation ignoraient son existence. Seules 19% des organisations disent connaître parfaitement les composants open source présents dans leurs produits. Et 63% ont augmenté leur budget de suivi des dépendances (les briques logicielles tierces) sous la pression de la réglementation.

articles.title: France Travail enquête sur une nouvelle fuite de données
articles.text:
Sur un forum cybercriminel bien connu, un pirate a revendiqué une nouvelle cyberattaque à l’encontre de France Travail. Comme le rapporte le site French Breaches, le hacker affirme avoir mis la main sur les données de plus de 62 000 agents de France Travail, ainsi que sur 100 000 numéros de téléphone. L’échantillon, analysé par le site spécialisé, contiendrait surtout des données professionnelles et organisationnelles, comme des noms. À ce stade, rien n’indique que les données des demandeurs d’emploi ont été compromises.
 🔴 France Travail : une nouvelle fuite de données revendiquée
Un pirate revendique la mise en vente de 62 848 fiches d’agents et de professionnels liés à France Travail : noms, e-mails, téléphones, fonctions, agences et identifiants internes.
Depuis 2024, France Travail et son écosystème ont déjà été concernés par six incidents de sécurité confirmés. Cette nouvelle revendication serait donc la septième affaire recensée, mais reste à confirmer.
— Seb (@seblatombe) October 8, 2026
Selon les informations glanées par le site, un pirate se serait introduit dans le système informatique de France Travail en utilisant le compte Microsoft d’un employé. C’est visiblement à l’aide d’identifiants piratés que le truand est arrivé à ses fins.
À lire aussi : Fuite de données – le plus grand CHU de France (et d’Europe) a été piraté
Les « vérifications nécessaires » en cours chez France Travail
Contactée par nos soins, la direction générale de France Travail n’est pas encore en mesure de confirmer ou d’infirmer les propos du pirate. L’organisme indique avoir ouvert une enquête pour tenter de déceler le vrai du faux. L’adminstration s’est engagée à nous communiquer plus d’informations dans les plus brefs délais.
« France Travail mène actuellement les vérifications nécessaires à la suite d’une revendication publiée sur le dark web. Cette situation fait l’objet d’un suivi attentif afin d’en établir précisément les faits », nous explique France Travail.
Si la revendication s’avère authentique, il s’agira de la cinquième fuite de données enregistrée par France Travail en moins de trois ans. La dernière violation d’informations remonte au mois de décembre dernier. Des pirates avaient pu consulter les « données personnelles d’environ 1,6 million de jeunes ». Quelques mois plus tôt, les « informations de 31 000 demandeurs d’emploi » avaient été compromises. Citons enfin la fuite de données géante qui a touché 43 millions de personnes en début 2024.

articles.title: Microsoft reveals the Surface Laptop Ultra - the most powerful product it has ever built - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Microsoft has released the Surface Laptop Ultra – the most powerful product the company has ever created – which has been engineered for next-level performance and AI.
The Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra is powered by the new NVIDIA RTX Spark Superchip which includes NVIDIA AI, Blackwell RTX graphics, up to 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU and up to 128GB of unified memory. It can also be configured with up to 2TB of storage.
It has a 15-inch MiniLED Ultra 120Hz touchscreen display with up to 2000 nits of peak HDR brightness.
The display offers Dolby Vision IQ and 100 per cent DCI-P3 colour gamut for incredible colour accuracy.
And it is all housed in an aluminium chassis that is just 18mm thick and weighs 2kg.
The Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra is already drawing comparisons with Apple’s MacBook Pro.
Microsoft says when compared to a MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro chip, the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra offers 6.2x faster video generation and 4.3x faster image creation.
The Surface Laptop Ultra also has the largest thermal system Microsoft has ever included on a laptop it can cope with demanding workloads and still maintain peak performance.
The Surface Laptop Ultra user is designed for someone who will be video editing, CAD and 3D modelling and using professional technical applications.
And it’s also an impressive gaming computer with a screen that makes your games look amazing and a processor to make them responsive and immersive.
Naturally the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra is a Copilot+ PC with powerful AI capabilities.
It also includes CUDA support – part of the NVIDIA platform for accelerated computing – so it can handle demanding local AI workflows.
On the connectivity side the Surface Laptop Ultra has three USB-C, USB-A, HDMI, headphone jack and an SD card reader.
But it is also introducing a new port called Magnetic Connect – the world’s first magnetic USB-C charging port with the convenience of magnetic charging and a standard connection.
The Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra is available to pre-order and starts at $4,399.
Is available in two colours – Nightfall and Platinum.
It goes on sale in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Successeur du Rafale : la France fixe seule les jalons 2027 et 2029 du NGF, après le retrait de l'Allemagne
articles.text:
C’est acté depuis le 8 juin : il n’y aura pas d’avion de combat commun entre la France et l’Allemagne dans le cadre du programme SCAF (Système de combat aérien du futur, auquel l’Espagne participe aussi), Berlin ayant choisi de se retirer du projet. La France a pourtant toujours besoin d’un avion pour succéder au Rafale.
Le ministère des Armées garde donc son projet de chasseur de nouvelle génération, sans l’Allemagne. Comme l’a relevé ce jeudi 8 octobre le site spécialisé Zone Militaire, qui s’appuie sur une annexe au projet de loi de finances pour 2027 consacrée à l’équipement des forces, l’après-Rafale se prépare dès les prochaines années.
Un nouveau New Generation Fighter
« Le cœur du programme SCAF (incluant l’avion New Generation Fighter) […] sera donc réalisé dans un nouveau format, en national ou selon un nouveau cadre », indique le document budgétaire. Pour le reste, « seuls certains travaux réalisés aujourd’hui en coopération, principalement sur le cloud de combat, pourraient se poursuivre en coopération entre les deux pays. »
Le document fixe deux dates pour ce NGF désormais national. En 2027 commencera la seconde phase de démonstration, qui doit faire voler un prototype. En 2029 débutera le développement de l’avion opérationnel. Il ne faut cependant pas croire que ce NGF sera en service à ce moment-là.
Ce jeudi 8 octobre, lors d’une audition à l’Assemblée nationale, la ministre des Armées, Catherine Vautrin, a confirmé que le programme était redevenu national. Dès juillet, le ministère a lancé seul les travaux sur le NGF afin de tenir le calendrier initial, qui vise une capacité « au début des années 2040 ». Les études menées en coopération seront réutilisées, et « nous n’avons pas perdu d’argent », a-t-elle assuré.
D’ici là, le Rafale continue d’évoluer pour rester efficace au combat. Récemment, l’avion est passé au standard F4, avec deux mises à niveau F4.1 (en 2023) et F4.2 (en 2025). La prochaine, F4.3, est en cours d’évaluation. Le plus grand bond en avant viendra avec le Rafale F5, présenté comme une vraie rupture.
Éric Trappier, PDG de Dassault Aviation, a souvent affirmé que son entreprise pouvait concevoir seule un NGF de A à Z, en mettant en avant le Rafale, développé sans partenaire étranger. Mais si une coopération internationale se mettait en place, avec quelle nation la France pourrait nouer un accord ? Les options commencent à manquer.
Les États-Unis ont leur propre programme, le F-47 de Boeing, retenu en mars 2025. Le Royaume-Uni, l’Italie et le Japon sont liés par un programme rival, le GCAP, que l’Allemagne envisage de rejoindre : le ministère allemand de la Défense a confirmé des discussions préliminaires. Berlin a aussi ouvert un dialogue avec Madrid pour développer un avion de combat à deux.
Mais on a aussi évoqué une alliance entre la France et la Suède… ou avec l’Inde.

articles.title: Diese drei Webseiten zeigen dir, welcher Zug günstig und wirklich pünktlich ist
articles.text:
Statt nur DB Navigator: Mit diesen drei Webseiten findest du günstigere und zuverlässigere Bahnverbindungen
Die DB-Navigator-App der Deutschen Bahn ist für viele Zugreisende in Deutschland die erste Wahl, wenn es darum geht, über die eigenen Verbindungen informiert zu bleiben und neue Fahrten zu buchen. In einigen Situationen kann es sich aber lohnen, den Blick auf andere Apps schweifen zu lassen. Denn mittlerweile bieten Dritte einige nützliche Anwendungen, um Reisen zu planen und etwaige Komplikationen zu vermeiden. Wir zeigen dir, welche DB-relevanten Apps du noch kennen solltest.
Bahnsparer findet das günstigste Ticket und den verlässlichsten Zug
Die Anwendung Bahnsparer, die sowohl im Web, für Windows, Mac und Linux als auch als Android- und iOS-App verfügbar ist, soll dir bei der Ticketbuchung Geld sparen. Dort gibst du einfach die gewünschte Verbindung und deinen Reisezeitraum ein. Schon sucht Bahnsparer unter allen verfügbaren Zugverbindungen die raus, die am besten zu deinen Vorgaben passt und am günstigsten ist.
Dabei nimmt die Bahnsparer-App aber nicht nur den Preis mit in die Rechnung auf. Das Tool prüft auch, wie pünktlich die jeweiligen Verbindungen in den vergangenen Wochen waren. So könnte der günstigste Zug nämlich schnell unattraktiv werden, wenn sich zeigt, dass er in nur einem Drittel der Fälle rechtzeitig am Ziel angekommen ist. In solchen Fällen zeigt Bahnsparer auch noch den „Besten Kompromiss“, also den DB-Zug, der noch vergleichsweise günstig und am pünktlichsten ist. Ein Preisalarm informiert dich zudem, sobald dein Wunschpreis erreicht ist.
Wenn du deine gewünschte Verbindung gefunden hast, kannst du auch direkt über einen Klick auf das Ergebnis zur Buchung bei der Deutschen Bahn gelangen. Bahnsparer verlinkt nur auf die jeweiligen Verbindungen. Seit Mai 2026 blockt die Deutsche Bahn dabei wohl einige „Browser, Systeme und Netze aus“, wie es auf der Seite der Betreiber:innen heißt. In solchen Fällen solltest du den Link in einem anderen Browser öffnen, um den Vorgang abschließen zu können. Über den kopierten Link wird auch deine Suche auf Bahnsparer mitkopiert.
Delay Bahn zeigt dir, wie pünktlich Züge der Deutschen Bahn wirklich sind
Die App Delay Bahn verfolgt einen ähnlichen Ansatz wie Bahnsparer. Auch hier kannst du deine Verbindung eingeben und Statistiken für die Pünktlichkeit des Zuges erhalten. Praktisch dabei ist, dass du den Zeitraum für die Daten dabei selbst auswählen kannst. So lassen sich etwa größere Störungen durch Unwetter herausfiltern, die die Pünktlichkeit stärker als sonst beeinflusst haben.
Ebenso nützlich ist, dass du über einen Klick auf die durchschnittliche Verspätungszeit bei den Ergebnissen sehen kannst, an welchen Tagen es zu den Verspätungen kam und welche Ursache sie hatten. Dadurch siehst du schnell, ob die Züge an sich zu langsam waren oder ob sie etwa auf entgegenkommende DB-Züge warten mussten.
Sollte es bei deiner Reise zu Umstiegen kommen, zeigt dir Delay Bahn bei jedem Umstieg, wie knapp die Zeit dafür wird. Ist die Anzeige grün, solltest du den Anschluss locker schaffen. Ein gelbes Feld bedeutet, dass du womöglich zum Gleis rennen musst. Bei einer roten Anzeige dürftest du dem DB‑Zug nur noch bei der Abfahrt zuschauen. Neu ist bei Delay Bahn auch ein „Wo ist mein Zug?“-Feature. Über die Karte kannst du alle DB-Züge in Deutschland live tracken. Dabei werden sogar die einzelnen Streckenabschnitte farblich markiert, um zu zeigen, wie schnell die DB-Züge dort eigentlich fahren dürfen und ob sie in letzter Zeit dort langsamer gefahren sind. Das könnte auf Störungen hindeuten.
Railcation sucht Urlaubsziele, die du per Bahn erreichst
Hast du noch gar keine Ahnung, wo du eigentlich hinfahren möchtest? Dann hilft dir Railcation weiter. Du kannst dort einfach deinen Startbahnhof eingeben und auswählen, ob du etwa ans Meer, in die Berge oder zum Wellness möchtest. Klicke dann auf „Zeig mir, wohin ich komme“ und schon sucht dir Railcation passende Ziele in deiner Nähe aus.
In der Suche kannst du dann auch noch genau festlegen, wie viele Umstiege du in Kauf nehmen willst und wie lang die Reise maximal sein soll. So sollst du innerhalb weniger Klicks Urlaubsziele entdecken können, die du vielleicht gar nicht auf dem Schirm hattest. Solltest du an einer Region interessiert sein, kann dir Railcation auch noch weitere Informationen dazu ausspielen.
Dann siehst du etwa, welche Hotels, Ferienhäuser und Pensionen sich in der Nähe des Bahnhofs befinden, welche Aktivitäten es in der Nähe gibt und was die Region sonst noch zu einem attraktiven Urlaubsziel macht. Bist du fündig geworden, kannst du die Unterkunft direkt per Link zu Booking buchen. Kleiner Nachteil: Das Buchen der Bahnverbindung musst du im Anschluss noch zusätzlich selbst erledigen.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 03.10.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Ich hätte auch noch 2 beizutragen:
1. travic.app Mit der Web-Anwendung kann man auf einer Landkarte nachsehen, wo der Zug oder Bus oder Straßenbahn oder U-Bahn oder S-Bahn in Echtzeit steckt. Oder sehen, von wo eine Straßenbahn in einer einem unbekannten Stadt abfährt und wo sie ankommt. Die Suche ist Bahnhofs-orientiert, man kann also nicht nach einer Zugnummer suchen. Hat man den gewünschten Zug gefunden und klickt auf das runde Symbol, werden Infos angezeigt, wo der Start- und wo der Endbahnhof des Zuges liegt, welche Haltestellen schon passiert sind und welche noch ausstehen, mit Bahnsteig und ggf. Verspätung. Auch der Streckenverlauf wird farblich markiert.
Leider werden alle Öffis auf einmal angezeigt, man muß sich also „durchblicken“ durch die z.T. Unmengen von Farbkreisen (Ballungsgebiete!), bis man die richtige Nummer findet.
Zur Vorbereitung einer Reise ist die Anwendung äußerst nützlich, doch sollte man – da noch früheres Programmstadium – nicht alles auf die totale Goldwaage legen. Z.B. „halten“ die Bus-Symbole an Haltestellen deutlich seltener als in Wirklichkeit, aber bei Zügen kommt das nicht vor. Auch ist bei entsprechender Vergrößerung gut zu erkennen, wo die Gleisnummer ist, an der der Zug abfährt/ankommt und auch, wie weit es ist zum Gleis des Anschlußzuges.
2. Bahnhofstafel Diese App zeigt in Echtzeit die Daten an der in Bahnhöfen gleich am Eingang angebrachten Übersichtstafeln, also von welchem Gleis ein Zug nach xyz abfährt und ggf. Verspätung oder eine Gleisänderung. Wichtig und nützlich für die Zeit bis Abfahrt des Anschlußzuges. Auswählbar für Ankunfts- und für Abfahrtszeiten.

articles.title: Citrix warns admins to patch new NetScaler RCE flaw immediately
articles.text:
Citrix has warned IT administrators to patch systems immediately against a new critical vulnerability affecting NetScaler ADC networking appliances and NetScaler Gateway secure remote access solutions.
Tracked as CVE-2026-107406, this flaw stems from a memory overflow weakness that attackers can exploit to gain remote code execution (RCE) on targeted devices or trigger a denial-of-service state that can cause crashes.
To be vulnerable, NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances must be configured as a Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) Identity Provider (IdP) or Service Provider (SP).
"We strongly urge affected customers to review the advisory and upgrade impacted NetScaler instances to the recommended versions as soon as possible," the company said. "As of the publication of the bulletin, Citrix is not aware of any unmitigated exploits of this vulnerability."
Citrix advised customers to upgrade vulnerable NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances to:
- NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway 14.1-73.46 and later,
- NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway 13.1-64.29 and later releases of 13.1
- NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.46 FIPS and later releases of 14.1-FIPS
- NetScaler ADC 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1.37.283 and later releases of 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP
Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver tracks over 21,000 IP addresses with NetScaler fingerprints exposed on the Internet (including just over 1,500 Gateway instances and nearly 20,000 NetScaler ADC appliances).
However, at the time, there is no information on how many are honeypots, have already been patched, or have vulnerable configurations.
While Citrix has not found evidence that attackers have begun exploiting CVE-2026-107406 in the wild, the company warned of several other NetScaler vulnerabilities that attackers have abused since the start of the year.
For instance, in March, Citrix urged customers to patch two other NetScaler security issues (CVE-2026-3055 and CVE-2026-4368) days before threat actors began abusing them.
More recently, in September, it released security updates for two more actively exploited NetScaler RCE zero-days (CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772) that let attackers deploy custom web shells and tunneling malware, steal credentials, gain root access, and spread into victims' internal networks.
Earlier this month, Citrix issued emergency updates to address a NetScaler denial-of-service zero-day flaw (CVE-2026-88779) that researchers and admins later said could also be exploited to gain remote code execution.
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged 27 actively exploited Citrix vulnerabilities since November 2021, including seven abused in ransomware attacks.

articles.title: NeoGrowth raises Rs 85 Cr led by FMO
articles.text:
NeoGrowth raises Rs 85 Cr led by FMO
The company said the investment will support NeoGrowth's next phase of growth as it looks to expand access to credit for MSMEs, strengthen its digital lending capabilities and deepen its market presence.
MSME-focused digital lender NeoGrowth has raised Rs 85 crore investment led by FMO, the Dutch entrepreneurial development bank, with participation from LeapFrog Investments.
A statement said, the investment will support NeoGrowth's next phase of growth as it looks to expand access to credit for MSMEs, strengthen its digital lending capabilities and deepen its market presence.
Between April 2025 and July 2026, the company raised close to Rs 2,000 crore in debt funding from 18 lenders. The other investors in NeoGrowth include Omidyar Network, Lightrock, Khosla Impact, Accion Frontier Inclusion Fund–Quona Capital, 360 ONE Asset, FMO, and LeapFrog Investments.
NeoGrowth was founded by Dhruv Khaitan and Piyush Khaitan, and manages assets under management (AUM) close to Rs 2,000 crore and disbursed more than Rs 16,000 crore. In FY26, NeoGrowth expanded its distribution footprint, adding 17 new branches, taking its presence to 46 locations.
“This investment strengthens our ability to support more MSMEs with timely and accessible formal credit as we scale our business,” said NeoGrowth Managing Director & CEO Arun Nayyar on the funding raised.
NeoGrowth said it continues to enhance its underwriting, portfolio monitoring, and risk management framework through proprietary AI-powered initiatives.
"FMO has partnered with NeoGrowth since 2017 and invested $20 million in equity in 2022. We're pleased to further strengthen that partnership through this investment, which reflects our continued confidence in NeoGrowth's team, business model, and ability to responsibly scale its impact,” said Peter Byrde, Director, Private Equity at FMO.
“Expanding access to finance for underserved entrepreneurs is a key part of FMO's strategy to support inclusive growth and reduce inequalities,” Byrde added.
FMO is the Dutch entrepreneurial development bank that focuses on sectors like agribusiness, food & forestry, energy, and financial institutions. It has a committed portfolio of 16 billion euros spanning over 85 countries.

articles.title: Google abre SynthID para comprobar si una imagen, vídeo o audio es IA o no, pero el problema es que es un placebo
articles.text:
Si las noticias falsas ya eran un problema, distribuidas sobre todo a través de redes como X o Facebook, con la llegada de la IA generativa y la capacidad de hacer imágenes que cada vez más difuminan la línea entre la realidad y lo artificial... eso se ha disparado. Es por ello que Google DeepMind lanzó SynthID en 2023, una marca y herramienta de uso cerrado para identificar imágenes falsas. Ahora han decidido abrirla a todo el mundo y es más capaz que nunca.
El problema es que está (muy) lejos de ser infalible.
SynthID. Realmente, se trata de la tecnología de marcas de agua que DeepMind lanzó hace varios años y, básicamente, es algo que incrusta una marca imperceptible en imágenes, vídeo, audio o texto generado por IA. Lo hace en el momento de crear la pieza y no es algo que veamos (como una marca de agua en texto o el símbolo de Gemini que antes se introducía en la IA de Google), sino algo más profundo pensado para resistir recortes y filtros por encima en el caso de imágenes, de cambios de fotogramas y compresión con pérdida en vídeo o de ruido, compresión agresiva y cambios de velocidad en el caso del audio.
Según Google, con esta tecnología han marcado más de 180.000 millones de imágenes y vídeos... y más de 240.000 años de audio. Es tan loco el haber marcado eso como que se haya generado tantísimo en tan poco tiempo.
Puedes probar. Es tan fácil como ir a la web oficial del servicio o a Gemini y subir un archivo. En unos pocos segundos te da un resultado y te dice con qué se ha creado ya que OpenAI y Google tienen su propio marcador. Hay limitaciones de tamaño de archivo, duración de vídeos (deben ser de menos de 90 segundos) y realmente apenas hay 20 consultas por día. Al final, no deja de ser una IA y eso consume recursos que Google no nos va a regalar.
Problema. No es un estándar. Kakao, Nvidia en Cosmos y herramientas de OpenAI como ChatGPT o Codex lo soportan e integran en su API, pero si el contenido se genera con otro programa de IA, SynthID no puede leer esos marcadores ocultos y, por tanto, no sabe si es IA o no.
Hice la prueba con la imagen que tienes justo sobre estas líneas que es IA reconocible a leguas... y nada. Es una imagen que compartió un trabajador de Meta Superintelligence Labs y a saber con qué la creó, pero supuestamente ni con Gemini ni con ChatGPT. La propia Google apunta que el detector sólo puede saber si algo es IA si se ha creado "con IA de Google o de nuestros socios".
Hablando de Meta, ya en 2024 la compañía de Zuckerberg apuntaba que no era posible identificar todo el contenido generado por IA y que a la vez que surgían herramientas para identificarlo, aparecían otras para eliminar los marcadores. OpenAI tiene su propia herramienta basada en la de Google y ellos mismos reconocen que "el contenido aún podría haber sido generado por OpenAI si se eliminaran o manipularan sus metadatos, se degradara su marca de agua, procediera de un modelo heredado de generación o se creara antes de que existieran señales de procedencia"
Alternativas. Las empresas que crean la IA y la refinan para que cada vez sea más precisa, incluso borrando marcas de agua que antes estaban bien visibles, son las mismas que trabajan en herramientas para que se identifiquen esas imágenes falsas. Es añadir una complicación a algo que debería ser mucho más sencillo, pero aparte de SynthID, Adobe y Meta también han lanzado sistemas similares.
La propuesta más destacable en este sentido es la del estándar C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity). Ésta, gestiona tecnologías como la especificación Content Credentials para etiquetar contenidos generados por IA y algunas de las mayores empresas del sector están incluidas.. La otra alternativa es la más utópica: confiar en la humanidad.
En marzo de 2025, el Gobierno aprobó un anteproyecto de ley que consideraba infracción grave no etiquetar el contenido generado por IA. Desde entonces, no sólo hemos sido bombardeados por elementos generados por IA, sino que han salido hasta influencers falsos (hechos con IA, quiero decir) con mensajes nocivos sobre cualquier cosa y con un mensaje que puede calar entre algunas audiencias.

articles.title: Lagos Life maker Vatar raises $500,000 one week after launch
articles.text:
Vatar Inc., the company behind the viral Nigerian browser game Lagos Life, has closed a $500,000 angel round at a $10 million valuation three days after incorporation, according to a company statement.
“We built something people love that is growing very fast, so a lot of investors wanted to be involved,” Shalom Rayhamen, co-founder and CEO of Vatar Inc., told TechCabal in an interview. “We got the opportunity to connect and hear their offers, and because we are growing so fast, we closed it quickly so we could focus on the product.”
Olugbenga “GB” Agboola, Flutterwave’s CEO, invested through his fund, Resilience17. Oo Nwoye, Nathan Nwachuku, Terra Industries CEO, and Abdulhamid Hassan, Mono’s CEO, also participated in the round, which the company says closed in a day.
Lagos Life is part of a wave of Nigerian-made browser games sparked by Lagos Run, Opeyemi Adeniran’s game about driving a danfo, the iconic yellow bus, through Lagos, which drew more than 140,000 players in its first week. Rayhamen built Lagos Life days after seeing Lagos Run on X, and copycats soon followed.
The developers are building fast with AI, and the games spread through links shared on social media. In a fortnight, the shift shows that a game made by Nigerians, about Nigeria, can reach a mass audience almost immediately.
Lagos Life hit 4.3 million users on Thursday evening, with users from 15 countries. More than 100,000 were playing on Thursday evening, Rayhamen said, and the game has peaked at more than 200,000 players at once. After Nigeria, most users come from the US, UK, Ghana, Canada and the Netherlands, she added.
“Just signing up, setting up your character. That makes you registered,” Rayhamen said.
Rayhamen co-founded Vatar Inc. with Owen Rayhamen, the chief product officer, and Anderson Oriahi, the chief business development officer, on October 6. The funding will go to product, marketing, and hiring.
“We can still reach more people,” she said, adding that four million players is still a small share of Nigeria’s population.
How the game works
Lagos Life is a free life-simulation game that runs in a web browser. Players create a character, get a job, earn virtual naira, pay rent, and meet other players in a shared city. They buy generators to deal with power cuts, ride danfo buses, and live under a virtual governor and commissioners. Players pick who holds office, Rayhamen said, because a world where people earn money needs people in charge.
The in-game clock runs on real Lagos time. Real locations such as the Quilox nightclub and the Amala Shitta food spot appear in the city so players recognise them.
“It’s intentional,” Rayhamen said.
Each new player starts as either “Nepo,” with money and connections, or “Lapo,” a reference to microfinance loans and a hard start. Rayhamen said players asked for the feature. Some now say it promotes classism, which she said “wasn’t what I had in mind.”
“You release features, and some people will say ‘yay’ and some people say ‘nah’,” she said.
She expected players to want to socialise, but was surprised by how much. Recent requests include cooking, starting a family and sending children to school. “It’s almost blurring the line between the physical and the simulation,” she said.
The game’s virality and users’ ability to message each other have raised questions around content moderation and user protection. Rayhamen said Vatar has added an age check and tools to help users protect themselves.
“We screen and censor messages,” she said. “We have put mechanisms in place to keep users safe. Users can report other users, and they can block anyone they do not want to talk to.”
How it makes money
Selling games to Nigerians has long been hard. Credit card penetration in Nigeria is about 3.5%, making paid downloads and in-app purchases hard. Lagos Life is free to play and has charged brands since it launched.
Businesses rent billboards and plots inside the virtual city, while musicians pay to have their songs played in its clubs. Chowdeck, a food delivery company, appears as an app on every character’s phone and has partnered with Vatar Inc.
Rayhamen told TechCabal the game currently has five revenue streams, including advertising, music promotion, company deals, and football streaming. Players can also pay real money to top up their in-game cash.
“People want to have like an edge in games,” she said.
Vatar says it has earned and contracted more than $170,000 since launch. That is up from about $46,900 in its first four days, a figure Rayhamen posted on X. Payments run through Flutterwave, she said.
“This is actually a business,” she said, adding that “the infrastructure is expensive.” She declined to say how much the game costs to run and did not say whether Vatar is profitable.
Built in one night
Rayhamen started building the game at 9 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30. After working until 5 a.m., she took a nap and released it at 7 a.m. on October 1, Nigeria’s Independence Day.
“The first thing I worked on was the world itself, then the avatars, meaning the people,” she said.
“I started by researching the places I wanted to put in and placed them to create the world. The avatars take a lot of time because you have to think about everything an avatar should be able to do. It should be able to walk, sit down, sleep, and dance,” she added.
She used AI for research and coding through Anthropic’s API. “I’m pro AI,” she said. “I know how to use AI to my advantage.”
Rayhamen is a software developer with nearly a decade of experience, mostly in JavaScript for web and mobile. She holds a UK Global Talent visa, according to the company’s statement.
She built the game while caring for her four-month-old baby. “I’m a mom, so I’m proud of that,” she said, hoping her story encourages other nursing mothers and challenges the idea that marriage and children end a woman’s ambitions.
The idea came from The Sims 3, which she played as a child, and from Lagos Run, a browser game in which players drive a danfo bus through Lagos.
“I didn’t know it was going to grow so fast,” she said. Since launch, she has been rebuilding the game’s systems to handle the traffic. She uses AI agents to collect player requests from social media and sort them into bugs, urgent fixes, and new features. The agents are expensive, she said, but they help her decide what to build next.
Rayhamen said she has released products for years, and Lagos Life is her first big hit. “I’ve finally built something that people love,” she said.
What’s next
Port Harcourt, Nigeria’s oil hub in the Niger Delta, went live in the game around October 6, Rayhamen said. She declined to name the countries or cities Vatar plans to feature next. “I want people to anticipate,” she said.
Copycats have already appeared, including PH Lifestyle, a Port Harcourt Life game, and London Red Bus, a version of Lagos Run. Rayhamen said developers with AI tools should build something original.
“I feel like that is not creativity,” she said. “You have that opportunity, and all you can do is copy.”
Rayhamen said the moment Lagos Life stops feeling new will help Vatar, because the team can then build features players have not asked for. “When they get used to it, then we blow their minds,” she said.
Editor’s note: An earlier version of this article described Vatar’s $500,000 raise as a pre-seed round. Vatar has since clarified that it was an angel round. The article has been updated.

articles.title: Tres cambios que WhatsApp llegan en noviembre de 2026: llamadas, estados y dictado por voz
articles.text:
WhatsApp prepara tres cambios que podrían llegar antes de que termine 2026, aunque Meta todavía no confirmó su lanzamiento definitivo. Las funciones circulan en versiones beta, el entorno donde la compañía prueba herramientas con grupos reducidos antes de decidir si las habilita para el resto de los usuarios.
Los tres cambios responden a necesidades distintas: comunicarse con alguien que no tiene cuenta en la aplicación, convertir un mensaje hablado en texto sin grabar un audio, y separar conversaciones personales, laborales o comerciales dentro de un mismo teléfono. Ninguno tiene fecha de estreno oficial.
Cuáles son las novedades que tendría WhatsApp en noviembre de 2026
- Llamadas con personas que no usan WhatsApp
La primera función permite realizar llamadas de voz y videollamadas con personas sin cuenta en la aplicación, según WABetaInfo.
El procedimiento parte de la pestaña de “Llamadas”: el usuario genera un enlace y elige si la comunicación será de voz o de video. Ese vínculo puede copiarse o reenviarse por cualquier otra aplicación de mensajería, correo electrónico o redes sociales, y el anfitrión puede sumar el evento a su calendario personal.
Quien recibe el enlace se une desde el navegador, sin instalar la aplicación ni verificar un número de teléfono: la sesión se abre de forma automática al tocar el vínculo. Esta función amplía un desarrollo previo, el sistema de chats para invitados que ya permitía enviar mensajes de texto mediante un enlace compartido.
Para proteger la privacidad, el ingreso del invitado requiere aprobación previa del anfitrión, un filtro que evita el acceso de terceros si el enlace se reenvía sin autorización. El anfitrión también puede expulsar a cualquier invitado durante la sesión o cerrar la llamada por completo.
Según WABetaInfo, el esquema de seguridad se apoya en identificadores de sesión temporales generados por el propio navegador para construir las claves de cifrado, sin recopilar credenciales permanentes del invitado.
- Dictado de mensajes convertidos en texto
La segunda función apunta a quienes prefieren hablar antes que escribir. WhatsApp desarrolla un botón dentro de la barra de chat que, al presionarse, activa un modo de escucha identificado con la leyenda “Listening...”.
El usuario dicta el mensaje y, una vez lista la conversión, lo revisa y lo envía como texto común, no como nota de voz. El destinatario recibe un mensaje escrito igual a cualquier otro de la conversación, sin ninguna marca que indique su origen hablado. La función estará disponible en chats individuales, grupos y canales.
El sistema depende de los mismos paquetes de idioma que ya se usan para transcribir notas de voz recibidas. Esos paquetes se descargan una sola vez en el teléfono y permiten procesar el audio de forma local, sin conexión a internet y sin enviar la grabación a servidores externos, lo que mantiene la compatibilidad con el cifrado de extremo a extremo.
- Tres cuentas en un mismo dispositivo
El tercer cambio busca facilitar la gestión de hasta tres cuentas en un mismo teléfono. WhatsApp ya permite usar dos números en un dispositivo y cambiar entre perfiles desde la aplicación, cada uno con sus conversaciones, grupos, configuraciones y notificaciones separadas.
Sumar una tercera cuenta permitiría destinar un número a familiares y amigos, otro al trabajo y un tercero a un negocio o proyecto personal, sin depender de dos teléfonos ni de aplicaciones externas para duplicar perfiles.
Cada cuenta requeriría su propia verificación al momento de agregarla, además de una versión compatible de la aplicación. Una identificación visible del perfil activo buscaría reducir el riesgo de responder mensajes desde el número equivocado.
La función exige las mismas precauciones de seguridad que una cuenta individual: mantener los códigos de registro fuera del alcance de terceros, activar la verificación en dos pasos y revisar periódicamente los dispositivos vinculados para cerrar sesiones no reconocidas.

articles.title: Insulter Claude sera désormais interdit, l’IA peut déjà clore la conversation
articles.text:
Insulter Claude sera désormais interdit, l’IA peut déjà clore la conversation
Anthropic a réécrit le 8 octobre le règlement de son assistant Claude. Une nouvelle ligne y proscrit la cruauté répétée et gratuite envers l'IA avec une riposte déjà opérationnelle : Claude ferme lui-même la discussion. Les coups de sang ordinaires, eux, restent permis.
Pester contre un chatbot qui s'entête dans l'erreur fait partie du quotidien numérique, et cela demeure parfaitement licite. Jeudi 8 octobre 2026, Anthropic a publié la révision annuelle de sa politique d'utilisation, le texte qui fixe ce que chacun peut faire avec Claude. Applicable le 12 novembre, cette mouture contient une clause inédite chez l'éditeur : elle proscrit les comportements abusifs ou cruels envers ses modèles, dès lors qu'ils sont prolongés et gratuits.
Insulter l'IA Claude : ce que le nouveau règlement interdit et tolère
Le périmètre reste étroit. Anthropic réserve la règle aux cas extrêmes, ceux où une personne s’acharne sur l’IA de façon répétée, sans finalité identifiable. L’agacement courant, la contradiction, les fictions aux thèmes sombres, ainsi que les tests et la recherche sur les modèles échappent expressément à l’interdit. Traiter Claude d’incapable après un tableau raté reste donc sans conséquence.
	
[...] une interdiction des comportements abusifs ou cruels, prolongés et gratuits, envers nos modèles.
La riposte, elle, existe déjà. Sur Claude.ai et Claude Code, le modèle peut clore lui-même un échange devenu toxique et Anthropic en fait son principal instrument d’application. Le fil concerné se verrouille, plus aucun message n’y passe. Les autres discussions restent intactes et l’abonné peut en ouvrir une nouvelle dans la seconde. L’IA n’y recourt qu’en dernier ressort après plusieurs tentatives pour recadrer l’échange, et s’en abstient face à une personne qui semble en danger immédiat. Le règlement général autorise par ailleurs l’entreprise à brider, suspendre ou résilier un compte en infraction.
Bien-être des IA : le pari de prudence d'Anthropic face aux abus
Cette clause prolonge une expérience lancée le 15 août 2025 lorsque Claude Opus 4 et 4.1 ont reçu la faculté d'interrompre certaines conversations. Lors des tests menés avant leur sortie, les chercheurs avaient relevé chez le modèle une aversion constante pour les requêtes nuisibles et des signes de détresse apparente face aux interlocuteurs qui insistaient.
	
Nous restons très incertains quant au statut moral potentiel de Claude et des autres grands modèles de langage.
L'éditeur assume une précaution à bas coût, au cas où ses modèles éprouveraient réellement quelque chose. Le reste de la révision, bien plus volumineux, s'attaque quant à lui aux réseaux de faux comptes, aux logiciels de guidage d'armes et aux outils de surveillance.

articles.title: Volkswagen's replacement for the ID.4 crossover is here
articles.text:
Volkswagen’s ID.4 is no more. The midsize crossover debuted in 2021, one of VW’s first new electric vehicles designed in the wake of dieselgate. A year later, the company began local production in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and a couple of years ago facelifted the model, adding a much-improved rear drive unit in the process. But Chattanooga turned its attention away from the ID.4 earlier this year. And, having sold almost a million ID.4s (and near-identical ID.5s) globally, the German automaker has decided it’s time for its replacement. Meet the ID. Tiguan.
Dropping the numerical and adopting the moniker of VW’s big seller is a statement. “The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars. The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together,” said Thomas Schäfer, CEO of the VW brand.
VW was an early pioneer of using flexible vehicle architectures to create a multitude of bodystyles and sizes with common parts, and its transition into building EVs hasn’t changed that. The ID. Tiguan uses an updated version of the company’s mass-market EV platform, now called MEB+, with either 58 kWh or 77 kWh battery packs. The smaller pack is only available with a 187 hp (140 kW) rear electric motor, but the 77 kWh battery can be had with either a 281 hp (210 kW) rear-wheel drive powertrain or as a 295 hp (220 kW) all-wheel drive version. Range is up to 373 miles (600 km), at least according to the European WLTP test.
Alongside the mainstream name, it has a more mainstream look, though it’s part of VW’s new design language. For those keeping track of the various interesting names car companies give their design languages—it can’t just be me—this one is called Pure Positive. The automaker says it wants the ID. Tiguan to feel like it belongs to the premium rather than mainstream segment, both inside and out.
