“Don’t use ‘open weight’ and ‘open source’ interchangeably”: Percona CEO on why AI terminology matters
articles.text:
“Don’t use ‘open weight’ and ‘open source’ interchangeably”: Percona CEO on why AI terminology matters
The AI industry has enthusiastically embraced the language of open source, even as some of its most prominent “open” models offer developers only a fraction of what that term has traditionally promised.
Speaking at Open Source Summit Europe in Prague on Wednesday, Peter Farkas, co-creator of the open source MongoDB alternative FerretDB and now CEO of open source database services company Percona, has a simple request: “Don’t use ‘open weight’ and ‘open source’ interchangeably,” he says.
“’Open source’ is only going to remain ‘open source’ as long as we preserve the actual meaning and the freedoms that are behind open source, and open weights are not providing that,” Farkas continues.
“’Open source’ is only going to remain ‘open source’ as long as we preserve the actual meaning and the freedoms.”
The distinction matters as open-weight models become a major part of production AI. In August, they accounted for 56% of tokens processed through Vercel’s AI Gateway and 60% of US-originating token consumption on OpenRouter, with Chinese-developed models accounting for the majority
An AI model’s weights are the numerical parameters produced during training that encode the patterns the model has learned. Making them available lets developers download and run a model on their own infrastructure, even when its creator hasn’t released the ingredients or process used to produce it.
“You don’t have the source code, you don’t have the training data, you only have the output of these two,” Farkas says. “So why would we call this open source in the first place?”
James Landay, director of Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), has drawn a similar distinction, arguing in an August HAI article that access to model weights alone falls short of what developers and researchers need from genuinely open-source AI.
“Open weights answer ‘can I run this?’” Landay said. “Open source answers ‘can I trust this, improve it, and build the next thing on top of it?’”
For now, Landay argues, the major AI labs are largely answering the first question while falling well short of the second.
“Open weights answer ‘can I run this?’ Open source answers ‘can I trust this, improve it, and build the next thing on top of it?’”
If “open washing wins”
Some companies are already going beyond releasing the weights. Xiaomi, for example, recently launched its MiMo-V2.6 models and livestreamed nearly a week of reinforcement-learning training through a public dashboard. The company also released more than 7,000 reinforcement-learning task environments, along with its RL training code and technical documentation, offering more transparency into how the models were fine-tuned.
Whether that’s enough for MiMo-V2.6 to qualify as “open source AI” is a separate question. Xiaomi’s release, however, illustrates the spectrum Farkas describes: “open” AI releases can reveal vastly different amounts of what went into building a model.
Farkas points to China’s DeepSeek as an example of the confusion, with its models widely described as open source despite the company releasing model weights rather than everything required to reproduce the models from scratch.
However, he stresses that the ability to download and run those models remains valuable in its own right.
“Are open weights a bad thing? No, open weights are great.”
“Are open weights a bad thing? No, open weights are great,” Farkas says. “You can run your models in your own environment, you can experiment with them, and if you understand the risks, you can also use it in production. The problem is when open weights are positioned as, ‘hey, this is as good as open source‘.”
Without a commonly understood boundary, Farkas argues, “open washing wins.” And he worries that accepting a looser meaning of open source for AI could ultimately weaken the definition for software more broadly.
“Companies are going to get away with calling something Apache 2.0 that [for example] you can’t use in the European Union,” Farkas says. “Open source AI is one thing, but if we talk about open source, and we let this happen to the core definition itself, that is going to go way beyond AI.”
A definition still under discussion
The Open Source Initiative (OSI) published its first Open Source AI Definition in 2024, establishing criteria around the freedoms to use, study, modify, and share AI systems. But the definition remains contested, particularly over what information about training data an AI system must disclose to qualify as open source.
Responding to Farkas from the audience, Duane O’Brien, who became the OSI’s new executive director in April, acknowledged the criticisms of its original definition and made clear that OSI is reopening the discussion.
“We did have a conversation two years ago — it was an important conversation, and two years is a long time in this space,” O’Brien says. “We are in the process of reopening and having another set of conversations.”
The OSI recently launched an Open Source AI Fellowship, appointing Gabriel Toscano as its first fellow to help build consensus around what constitutes open source AI. The two-year program will explore potential revisions to the definition, while OSI also plans a series of community discussions, or “open source salons,” over the next two years.
O’Brien encouraged Farkas and others to participate, while acknowledging the criticisms already leveled at the original definition.
“The criticisms that have been lodged against open source AI definition ‘one’ are valid,” O’Brien says. “We have to continue that conversation.”

articles.title: Pre-Baked Firmware Malware Hits Budget Android Devices in 150+ Countries
articles.text:
There is a large global market for low-cost Android devices. Bad actors are aware and are servicing the demand through devices built on MediaTek platforms – but with malware preinstalled in the device firmware.
When the recipient of such an affected device switches it on, the malware is present, unseen, and available to any bad actor who can control it remotely from its C2. It is a persistent, pre-installed firmware system app that cannot be removed by normal uninstall procedures.
The campaign, dubbed Midnight Mimosa, was discovered and analyzed by Bitdefender.
The potential for this type of malware infection controlled via the actor’s C2 is massive. “The malware runs with system-level privileges that allow it to silently install and remove apps, grant permissions, and load arbitrary code supplied remotely. This essentially means its operators could install and delete apps at will, tuning each device to their needs, including making them part of large botnets,” writes the Bitdefender report.
Midnight Mimosa is focused on ad fraud, automated click fraud, and turning the device into a single component of a much larger botnet. This makes sense for a campaign seeking to fly under the radar with an army of soldiers. Many thousands of click frauds over a period of time would provide a healthy ROI for any bad actor. And botnets are described as a hot commodity that can be rented out to other bad actors. The bigger the botnet, the better the bounty.
Over the last two years, Bitdefender has observed thousands of unique affected devices in more than 150 countries. No single country or region dominates distribution. Mexico and France lead, followed by Italy, US, Germany, Brazil and Spain. Regionally, Western Europe and the Americas stand out. The report gives no indication of the actual monetary gain achieved by the Midnight Mimosa operators but does provide an extensive list of IoCs to help prevent it.
Bitdefender also found 13 apps on Google Play with separate signing certificates under two developer accounts and containing the same Midnight Mimosa ad-fraud code. “The campaign is not confined to preinstalled firmware. Thirteen applications published on Google Play were found carrying the same family markers as the dropped cover apps, in builds distributed by Play itself,” note the researchers.
These Play Store apps do not have the same privileged access as the preinstalled malware, but are considered associated with the broader ecosystem, giving the attackers an additional distribution channel.
Whether the malware is preinstalled or loaded from Play Store, it has been seen disabling the Play Store before installing additional payload applications and then re-enabling it afterward – probably to avoid detection by Play Protect. “Beyond suppressing the install prompt, the plugins blind Google Play Protect for the duration of the install,” note the researchers. “The malicious install happens in a window where Google’s scanner is switched off.”
Midnight Mimosa is best considered as a supply-chain threat where malware is largely integrated into the Android device prior to sale. The campaign is characterized by preinstalled persistence, system-level control, ad-fraud activity, proxy-network abuse and remote payload management. Attackers have extensive control over affected devices from the get-go.

articles.title: John Cena ('Matchbox') compara la WWE con el cine de acción: "Las peleas en las películas son agotadoras"
articles.text:
Tras su paso por la WWE como uno de los luchadores más legendarios de la competición, John Cena irrumpió en Hollywood hace ya varios años para hacerse un nombre también como actor. Ahora es, de hecho, una de las grandes estrellas de la industria gracias a éxitos como Peacemaker o las sagas Fast & Furious y Transformers. Así, asume un nuevo reto, otra vez en el cine de acción y coches. Y es que acaba de estrenar en Apple TV Matchbox: la película.
En Hipertextual hemos podido entrevistarle a raíz de este reciente estreno, su segundo proyecto sobre una franquicia de juguetes de Mattel (recordemos que ya apareció brevemente en Barbie). Muy atento y dispuesto, se ha abierto de par en par sobre la película, pero también sobre su carrera. Y es que a lo largo de los años, además de en la comedia, John Cena se ha especializado en el cine de acción, como no podía ser de otra forma. Sin embargo, asegura que es algo muy distinto a la WWE.
"Es muy diferente. La coreografía en directo de la WWE me resulta muy fluida. Sabes que no vas a tener una segunda oportunidad. Casi no hay margen para el error. Si hay algún tropiezo, es en directo, así que es real. Es muy improvisado. Depende del intérprete con el que estés trabajando. Yo me consideraba más bien una persona de improvisación física. Y la historia se cuenta en menos tiempo", nos explica.
"De hecho, ¿sabes qué? Las peleas son tan cortas en las películas que parece que estuvieras peleando eternamente. Las escenas de acción en las películas, para mí, entrañan mucho menos riesgo. Porque las acrobacias espectaculares de la WWE no cuentan con cuerdas de seguridad. Es en directo, tal y como ocurre. Así que hay muchas variables que podrían surgir. Además, suele hacerse en un estadio ante el público. Así que hay muchas variables", comenta a su vez John Cena.
"La acción de las películas, como cuando [en Matchbox: la película] subo corriendo por el Puente de las Cadenas de Budapest o me cuelgo de un helicóptero, aunque me dé miedo, son totalmente seguras. Es solo cuestión de que un ser humano no debería hacer algo así y tienes que superar tus miedos. Pero es increíblemente seguro. Las peleas en las películas son agotadoras porque duran muchísimo. Hay que hacer muchísimas tomas de la misma coreografía una y otra vez desde diferentes ángulos", insiste.
"Mientras tanto, en la WWE suena la música, sales, haces lo tuyo, te diviertes, vuelves completamente agotado y, al mismo tiempo, lleno de energía porque decenas de miles de personas estaban súper emocionadas. Y luego lo vuelves a hacer la noche siguiente. Las peleas en las películas son preciosas y muy precisas, y se parecen mucho más a una danza en la que el ritmo, la sincronización y la distancia son fundamentales, mientras que en la WWE son un poco más fluidas", sentencia. En definitiva, y en contra de lo que pueda parecer a simple vista, para John Cena la acción de la WWE y la del cine no tienen nada que ver, son artes distintos.
Volver a Mattel
Con Matchbox: la película, como decíamos, John Cena regresa a Mattel. Esta vez como protagonista. Tras el éxito de Barbie, las expectativas podrían estar en tratar de alcanzar aquel fenómeno, algo a todas luces imposible. Pero el actor celebra la manera en la que la compañía entiende sus propios proyectos. "Esto es lo que me encanta de Mattel. Entienden que su propiedad intelectual es muy conocida. También comprenden el complejo proceso que supone tomar una propiedad intelectual que la gente conoce y con la que tiene cierta conexión, y luego llevarla a la gran pantalla en forma de película", sugiere.
"Cuando recibí el guion de Matchbox: la película, pensé: «¿Cómo demonios van a hacer esto? De niño me encantaba jugar con esos coches. Ya tengo una idea clara en mi mente de lo que es Matchbox. ¿Cómo van a trasladar mi pasión a la pantalla?». Pero cuando ves Matchbox: la película, no resulta para nada forzado", nos cuenta, orgulloso del filme.
"Y no teníamos a Mattel vigilándonos y diciendo: «Necesitamos más de esto». Son unos socios estupendos porque entienden que la propiedad intelectual ya existe y cuenta con una base de fans apasionados. El trabajo consiste en hacer una gran película. Tanto Barbie como Matchbox: la película son magníficos ejemplos de ello. Yo estuve presente en ambos rodajes y Mattel simplemente dejó que los creativos fueran creativos", prosigue John Cena.
"Estaría dispuesto a hacer cualquier cosa que quisieran adaptar, porque entienden que no tiene por qué ser una traslación exacta del juguete a la pantalla. Y creo que eso es muy importante desde el punto de vista de la propiedad intelectual como socio", concluye. Quién sabe, quizá en el futuro veamos una nueva película de Mattel protagonizada por John Cena. Al fin y al cabo la compañía cuenta con marcas de juguetes como Hot Wheels, Fisher-Price, Monster High o incluso las cartas del UNO.
La colección de coches de John Cena
Si hay algo que los fans querían ver en Matchbox: la película, son coches. Y precisamente John Cena es el mejor actor posible para encargarse del filme porque, en la vida real, su colección de coches es inigualable. El actor siempre ha sido un gran amante de la automoción y en su garaje tiene decenas de vehículos, algunos de ellos absolutamente históricos.
Por ello, le hemos preguntado por el coche que más le ha gustado conducir en Matchbox: la película y que le gustaría añadir a su colección. "El que más pude conducir fue el Land Rover 6x6. Por extraño que parezca, al fichar para formar parte de una película llamada Matchbox, pensé que iba a estar conduciendo todo el rato. Resulta que mis compañeros son los que conducen la mayor parte del tiempo y yo me encargo de la mayoría de las peleas cuerpo a cuerpo. Así que fue un poco agridulce, pero al menos pude conducir ese Land Rover", confiesa.
"Bueno, y hay un Chevy que también está bastante bien...", recuerda entonces. Se refiere a un Chevrolet Camaro de 1969 de color azul que se convierte en un genial macguffin de la película. "No quiero dar pistas que puedan ser spoilers ni nada por el estilo. Solo diré que hay un par de esos muscle cars americanos de gran potencia. He tenido la suerte de poder conducir algunos de esos coches y son muy divertidos porque tienen un motor realmente grande en un coche muy pesado e inestable, así que tienes que estar muy atento", dice a su vez.
Y en el sentido opuesto, John Cena también tiene claro qué coche de su colección privada se habría llevado a la película si le hubiesen dejado. "El primer coche que compré con mi propio dinero es un Jeep de 1989. Me hubiera encantado conducirlo por el desierto del Sáhara, simplemente porque ese coche me ha acompañado en prácticamente cada etapa de mi trayectoria profesional. Así que llevarlo al Sáhara y huir de los malos en él, con todo ese caos a su alrededor, eso habría sido ideal para el Jeep. Me habría ido de maravilla, me hubiera encantado darle un papel en la gran pantalla", confirma.
Matchbox: la película ya está disponible en Apple TV.

articles.title: Arc Raiders publisher developing AI anti-cheat stack in escalating war with cheaters — game license blacklisting and zero-second-chance permabans now standard
articles.text:
Arc Raiders publisher developing AI anti-cheat stack in escalating war with cheaters — game license blacklisting and zero-second-chance permabans now standard
There's no place for cheaters in Speranza.
The publisher behind Arc Raiders is now training in-house AI models to detect cheating as the arms race escalates with persistent cheaters. Cheating on online games is a perennial problem, and it only gets worse the more a title becomes popular, which is why the Arc Raiders developer released an update on its anti-cheat measures. According to Arc Raiders executive producer Aleks, Embark Studios has been working on the issue, and it has deliberately been scant on details to make it harder for cheat engine makers to adapt. However, this stance has been frustrating some players, which is why the company finally gave some details of what it has been working on behind the scenes.
Embark Studios said that it’s already using kernel-level anti-cheat from Denuvo, and that it also detects cheaters using Anybrain’s AI service. But aside from those third-party providers, the company said that it’s also using artificial intelligence to build in-house models to help detect cheating. “In addition to kernel-level protection from Denuvo and detections from Anybrain, we’re using a growing set of in-house models built around machine-learning and other data,” Aleks wrote. “These systems work together to identify suspicious behavior and build confidence before action is taken, while allowing us to continue improving detection as new cheats emerge.”
Aside from building and using anti-cheat tools, the developer is also tightening its enforcement of anti-cheating rules. A permanent ban is now the standard sanction for anyone caught cheating, and it will not give any warnings or second chances to offenders. It has also started associating copies of the game to accounts accused of cheating, so cheaters can’t simply make a new account using the same game license to get back into the game. Other accounts linked to a banned copy of the game will receive the same permaban, as well.
Aleks also said that Embark Studios is working on a hardware ban to cut the number of repeat offenders, and that it hopes to implement this solution later this year. This may be the biggest move that Embark Studios will make, but it also risks other players who buy used hardware that’s been previously flagged and get their account banned, too. One unfortunate Valorant player experienced this recently, but since Riot’s bans are temporary, they could get back into the game after a few months. This might be a different case for Arc Raiders, though, since the game enforces permabans, so this is something that it must consider so it doesn’t prosecute innocent gamers.
All these changes might seem harsh, but it seems that the crackdown is driven by complaints from the game’s burgeoning community. Aleks even noted some players’ frustrations, especially when they see streamers boasting their cheats, but said that the company is careful so that it doesn’t incorrectly ban legitimate players.
Anti-cheat technology is a game of cat and mouse between developers and cheaters, and Aleks said, “it will never fully go away.” Embark Studios is trying to make it as difficult as possible, though, and has employed these strict measures as a deterrent to prevent players from even thinking about cheating. It’s also not the only developer trying to clamp down on cheating, with an individual researcher even building a technique to fingerprint players using their mouse and keyboard inputs and track cheaters across accounts and hardware.

Jowi Morales is a tech enthusiast with years of experience working in the industry. He’s been writing with several tech publications since 2021, where he’s been interested in tech hardware and consumer electronics.

articles.title: Edmonton Startup Week panelists say AgTech could power the next tech boom | BetaKit
articles.text:
Founders looking to ride the wave of the next tech boom should look to AgTech, according to a group of panellists at Edmonton Startup Week.
Douglas Mills, the vice-president of external relations at the Canadian Agri-food Automation and Intelligence Network (CAAIN), told audiences during a panel discussion on opportunities within AgTech that the space was uniquely positioned to experience a boom in innovation, citing its tendency toward early adoption, lower regulatory thresholds, and hands-on validation.
“Whether you’re interested in AI, data, biotech, sustainability, advanced manufacturing, AgTech presents real-world problems that need innovative solutions.”
Douglas Mills, CAAIN
“[It’s] a sector rich with opportunity,” Mills said. “When we’re talking about agriculture, think broadly. We’re not just talking about a farm, tractor, or cows in a field. Think of opportunities across the whole value chain: animal health, logistics, transportation, solar, processing, value-add tools, machinery, analytics, robotics, computer vision, AI research, and biotech.
“It’s a massive sector when you’re looking at all the opportunities out there. Whether you’re interested in AI, data, biotech, sustainability, advanced manufacturing, AgTech presents real-world problems that need innovative solutions,” he added.
Mills was joined on stage by three others, including Colin Coros, the COO at precision diagnostics and medtech company Nanostics, BJ Fuchs, a cattle rancher and AgTech supporter, and David Bressler, the vice-president of international innovation and enterprise at the University of Alberta.
“One of the exciting things about Ag … is they’re leading technology. They’re early adopters,” said Coros. Prior to his role at Nanostics, he was the CEO of Delta Genomics, where he worked on livestock biobanking. Biobanking is the process of freezing and storing biological or genetic material to preserve agricultural diversity, or reconstitute livestock breeds.
“We think autonomous vehicles are coming one day, but they’ve already been in the agriculture sector for over a decade. There’s not a combine in Alberta that isn’t self-driven.
“It’s an industry where if there’s a solution, and they can increase productivity with it, they’ll adopt it, and they’ll adopt it faster than almost any other sector,” Coros added.
That makes the field particularly attractive to entrepreneurs, especially those looking to validate technology, or who are struggling to navigate complex regulatory requirements in a field like medtech or biotech. Coros said AgTech can be a useful stepping stone for both.
RELATED: Edmonton mayor hints at upcoming support for entrepreneurs as city’s Startup Week kicks off
“I talk to a lot of deep tech healthcare people … and you’re talking about going through a 15-year journey before you even get anything into the medical space,” he said. “If you really want to provide your technology, have you thought about livestock where maybe you can get this to market in five years, work out your kinks, and then maybe the next market is healthcare?”
That rule applies for tech startups who might not be in the traditional AgTech space. Fuchs, whose company Business Wide View has been involved in trialling innovations in real-world settings, said agricultural producers should be the first point of contact for anyone looking to see if their tech might have a dual-use purpose in the agricultural space.
“Sky’s the limit. Drones, water-trough monitors: there’s so much out there, and every operation is different,” Fuchs said. “If you have a great idea, talk to a producer; talk to more than one. It will give you answers around what the challenge is.”

articles.title: Zurich’s Klarent raises €7.13 million to scale its agentic software testing platform and expand into the US | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Klarent (formerly fore ai), a Zurich-based autonomous software testing startup, has closed a €7.13 million Seed funding round.
The round was led by London-based Mosaic Ventures, with participation from Moonfire Ventures and a number of prominent angel investors, including Jürgen Galler, a former Director at Google, Harris Barton, and AngelInvest Ventures, among others.
“With AI, code generation is scaling faster than our ability to test it, so QA will become the key bottleneck. Asheem and Momo saw this at Google before most of the industry did. What convinced us was their insistence on determinism – using AI to write tests, not to run them – which is why enterprises are trusting Klarent in production. We’re delighted to back the team as they expand to the US,” said Chandar Lal, Partner, Mosaic Ventures.
The startup was founded in 2023 by two ex-Google engineers, Asheem Panakkat, who serves as CEO, and Momchil Ivanov, who serves as CTO. Panikkar spent more than a decade at Google leading teams on Shopping and Lens, while Ivanov worked as a Staff Software Engineer focused on information retrieval. Together, they spotted how the explosion in code being written as large language models became more capable meant the systems used to verify that code were nowhere near ready to keep up.
Their solution: deterministic autonomy. Instead of leaning on large language models to run tests directly, Klarent’s agents use LLMs only to author test code. Once written, the test code executes in a deterministic, repeatable manner, combining the adaptability of AI with the rigour expected in production engineering. There is also a human-in-the-loop verification layer on top, ensuring customers pay only for verified outcomes.
“At Google, Momo and I could see two things coming at once: LLMs were getting better fast, and the amount of software being created was about to explode. The question that wouldn’t leave us was the feedback loop. How do you keep these coding agents honest? We began by building evals for LLMs and quickly realised the bigger opportunity was QA itself. As AI writes more of the world’s code, testing stops being a cost centre and becomes the thing that determines whether any of that code can be trusted,” said Panakkat.
Their approach has already won over enterprise clients across Europe. JD Sports, Swiss media group NZZ, and mobility company Sixt all use the platform. At JD Sports, Klarent’s AI agents automate multi-system workflows across the e-commerce pipeline, an automation that the retailer said its own teams could not replicate.
The funding will be used by Klarent to support its entry into the United States, building on the momentum seen with its European enterprise customers. The company also plans to grow its engineering team and broaden its cross-platform testing capabilities across web and mobile. It is also pushing into financial services, working with banks and insurance firms where the cost of a broken software release can be catastrophically high.

articles.title: ProArt GR1X : Asus promet 100 FPS en 1440p avec 140 watts sur son mini-PC RTX Spark, sans dire comment — Frandroid
articles.text:
Asus a donné ce jeudi 8 octobre de nouveaux détails sur son mini-PC ProArt GR1X. C’est un boîtier de 15 centimètres de côté, vendu jusqu’ici pour l’intelligence artificielle. Pourtant, sur sa fiche produit, le constructeur taïwanais promet aussi des jeux AAA (les grosses productions à gros budget) en 1440p à plus de 100 images par seconde (FPS). Et il annonce un TDP de 140 watts pour la puce entière, processeur et partie graphique compris. Sur un PC fixe, la carte graphique consomme souvent davantage à elle seule.
Le GR1X repose sur la puce RTX Spark de Nvidia. C’est un SoC (system on chip), qui réunit le processeur et la partie graphique sur une même puce. Nvidia et ses partenaires la vendent avant tout pour l’IA locale, avec des modèles qui tournent sur la machine sans passer par le cloud.
Asus présentait d’ailleurs le GR1X comme une machine à faire tourner des agents IA en local 24 heures sur 24. Les agents IA sont des assistants qui enchaînent des tâches tout seuls. Le communiqué publié par Asus le 8 octobre décrit encore toute la gamme ProArt RTX Spark comme conçue pour ce type d’IA.
Côté fiche technique, le GR1X a droit à la version la plus musclée de la puce. Elle associe un processeur Grace de 20 cœurs à une partie graphique Blackwell de 6 144 cœurs. Notebookcheck précise que la variante à 18 cœurs sera réservée aux PC portables. Le GR1X aura 64 ou 128 Go de mémoire unifiée LPDDR5X, que se partagent le processeur et la partie graphique.
Protégez votre vie numérique avec Bitdefender, la protection européenne de confiance. Bitdefender vous protège contre les arnaques et les fraudes du web. Profitez de vos activités en ligne en toute tranquillité.
Asus annonce aussi deux emplacements M.2 pour le stockage, sans dire de quelle capacité. Il y a aussi un port réseau à 10 Gb/s (dix fois le débit d’une prise Ethernet classique), du Wi-Fi 7 et la prise en charge de quatre écrans 4K. L’ensemble pèse 1,48 kg pour environ 1,1 litre de volume. Notebookcheck le compare d’ailleurs au Mac Studio d’Apple.
100 FPS, mais dans quels jeux et avec quels réglages ?
Asus ne précise ni les jeux utilisés ni les réglages graphiques derrière ses 100 FPS. Pourtant, sur la fiche produit, le chiffre est affiché juste à côté du logo DLSS. Cette technologie de Nvidia calcule l’image dans une définition plus basse, puis l’agrandit grâce à l’IA.
Sur la même page, Asus vante aussi la génération d’images multiples (Multi Frame Generation). Cette fonction insère des images créées par l’IA entre celles que la puce calcule réellement. Sur l’architecture Blackwell, elle peut multiplier jusqu’à six fois le nombre d’images affichées. En théorie, 17 images calculées par seconde suffiraient donc à en afficher 100 (le 1440p « natif » est loin).
Ce vendredi, le site Wccftech a repéré l’argument. Selon lui, la partie graphique de la RTX Spark ne peut pas atteindre 100 FPS en 1440p natif. Le site regrette aussi qu’Asus ne dise pas quels niveaux de mise à l’échelle et de génération d’images ont été utilisés. Pour l’instant, aucun test indépendant du GR1X en jeu n’a été publié.
Moins de watts qu’une RTX 5070 seule
La partie graphique de la RTX Spark a 6 144 cœurs. C’est autant qu’une GeForce RTX 5070 de PC fixe, une carte annoncée à 250 watts à elle seule. Le GR1X fait tenir le processeur et la partie graphique dans 140 watts. Pour le refroidissement, il compte deux ventilateurs et quatre caloducs (des tubes qui transportent la chaleur vers les ailettes).
Par contre, le même nombre de cœurs ne garantit pas les mêmes performances. La RTX 5070 dispose de sa propre mémoire GDDR7, alors que la RTX Spark partage sa LPDDR5X avec le processeur. On ne parle pas de la même bande passante mémoire. Et le TDP indique la chaleur que le refroidissement doit évacuer. Personne n’a encore mesuré la consommation réelle à la prise, et Asus fournit un bloc d’alimentation USB-C de 240 watts.
    Pour aller plus loin
Surface RTX Spark Dev Box : Microsoft lance son mini PC Nvidia pour l’IA locale
            
Asus n’est pas seul sur ce créneau. Microsoft vend son propre mini-PC RTX Spark pour l’IA locale, et la même puce équipe son Surface Laptop Ultra avec 128 Go de mémoire. De leur côté, AMD et Minisforum répondent avec un mini-PC à 192 Go de mémoire. Asus vend aussi l’Ascent GX10, une machine sous Linux pour les développeurs IA, basée sur le DGX Spark de Nvidia.
Asus n’a encore donné ni le prix ni la date de sortie précise du GR1X. Le mini-PC arrivera « plus tard cette année » chez une sélection de revendeurs haut de gamme, surtout en 64 et 128 Go.
Pour se faire une idée, les PC portables Asus ProArt P16 et P14 sont en précommande depuis le 7 octobre. Aux États-Unis, ils démarrent à 2 599,99 dollars (environ 2 320 euros HT). Chez Microsoft, chaque gigaoctet de mémoire supplémentaire se paie cher. Si c’est pour jouer, attendez les premiers tests en jeu avant d’acheter le GR1X et l’écran 1440p qui va avec.
    Pour aller plus loin
Surface Laptop Ultra : combien Microsoft facture-t-il vraiment le Go de mémoire ?

articles.title: a16z’s Olivia Moore on the state of consumer AI | TechCrunch
articles.text:
I wrote this week about the bleak economics of consumer AI — but where some see a crisis, others see an opportunity.
Olivia Moore covers consumer AI as a partner at Andreessen Horowitz — and on Monday, she released a report on the top 100 consumer AI apps. ChatGPT is still the biggest player by a mile, but smaller players like Suno and ElevenLabs are showing real staying power. Even more interesting is what we don’t see, as Moore’s report details half a dozen consumer categories that seem to be completely untouched by AI.
Moore sees a huge opportunity in consumer AI, particularly if the industry can tap into revenue streams beyond just subscriptions and API charges. On a call this week, I talked with her about the unusual economics of consumer AI and why it’s still early days for the category.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
It’s an interesting moment for a report about consumer AI, since we’ve seen OpenAI pivot back to enterprise this year. It’s inspired a lot of pessimism about the overall revenue picture for consumer AI, including from me. But I take it you’re more optimistic?
I agree with you that OpenAI has moved back towards the enterprise. To me, it’s not necessarily a pivot because they’re still launching a lot in consumer. It’s more of an expansion. But I don’t blame them, as much as I love consumer, because almost all of the AI revenue thus far has come from subscriptions and then token usage. And that is much more concentrated on the enterprise and prosumer side.
How can consumer AI products change that revenue problem? The State of Markets report reminded us that just 2.2% of U.S. households are paying for AI. Do we need that number to rise before the market becomes attractive?
I actually don’t know if I want to see that user number increase. I’m more interested in getting back to a world where the consumer is monetized in a way that isn’t subscription dollars out of their own pocket.
I think it’s very easy in Silicon Valley, with people who are high-income and have corporate cards to pay for those tools, to say, “oh well, I’d rather pay for the product.” But I think most people would actually rather have free access to something and see some ads, and then they can decide if they want to subscribe or not to make the ads go away.
The other challenge is the marginal cost of AI services, which is still a lot higher than classic internet services like Facebook or Google Search. Do you see a lot of these services finding ways to keep those costs down, whether it’s open source or other lightweight models?
Yeah, I think we’re seeing improvements there. Even ChatGPT now has a Go plan, which is just $8 a month, and I’m assuming it runs on cheaper models. We don’t necessarily need frontier intelligence for every task, and so that could mean cheaper models, especially for some consumer use cases. It could also mean more consumer companies building on top of open source models. We’ve heard a lot of that from our founders lately, and it really feels like it’s starting to change.
The problem is that right now, the users driving the revenue are doing coding and other technical automation, where they probably do need frontier intelligence. I think as we get more people building for the consumer, where the model is not the product, we’ll start to see lower-cost models used more often.
It’s unusual to talk about technical automation in a consumer service, which feels like another unique feature of AI. Are we starting to blur the lines between consumer and enterprise?
I wrote an article about this maybe a year or so ago called The Great Expansion trying to get at this. Pre-AI, you would have companies like Canva that were consumer-first and often took six or seven years to even add teams or enterprise plans. Now we’re seeing companies like Gamma, ElevenLabs, and Cursor that start as consumer and within 18 months become majority-enterprise businesses.
Almost all of what we think of as consumer AI, I would argue, is prosumer AI. This really comes out on the revenue list, where there’s basically like three categories that power users are spending on. There’s product-building apps, so like Lovable, Replit, and Fal. There’s product marketing, which is AI ad generators like Higgsfield or HeyGen. Then there’s general work management, like Manus, Fireflies AI, and Granola. Those are like being paid for by consumers to start with, but I would argue that they’re not consumer in the way that we would think about pre-AI.
There are also all these whitespace categories: social apps, dating apps, marketplaces, retail, travel, finance, health. There are no entrants in our top 100 list in those categories, which is pretty surprising. And that’s what I think we need to see over the next six months.
So maybe we haven’t really seen true consumer AI yet?
It’s definitely very early.

articles.title: Surfshark ‘proud’ to have backed Disinfo 2026 after governments pulled out under political pressure
articles.text:
Surfshark ‘proud’ to have backed Disinfo 2026 after governments pulled out under political pressure
The VPN said intellectual freedom remains crucial at a time when AI-generated content spreads misinformation
Surfshark has said it is proud to have backed Disinfo2026 after the EU’s diplomatic service, Canada and Lithuania pulled out of the event following political pressure.
On Thursday, the VPN issued a statement explaining its decision to continue sponsoring the annual event, which tackles disinformation and online deception, despite government sponsors withdrawing their support.
As further evidence of its commitment to intellectual freedom, the VPN – one of the best on the market – emphasised the importance of safeguarding the free exchange of ideas. “Open debate must never be silenced. It is essential for building a safer internet,” stressed the VPN.
A diplomatic issue
Organised by independent Brussels-based non-profit EU Disinfo Lab and held at a hotel in Vilnius, Lithuania, the two-day conference brought together hundreds of researchers, journalists, technologists and policymakers to collaborate on countering disinformation.
As reported by the Guardian, the Trump administration had pressured several countries to withdraw their sponsorship from the conference, prompting Canada, Lithuania, and the EU’s diplomatic service to retract their backing a few days before the event took place.
According to documents seen by the newspaper, the pressure centred on a panel discussion in which the US was reportedly regarded as “a foreign information threat.” The debate focused on how the European community, committed to combating disinformation, can strengthen its resilience without Washington; three US speakers took part in the debate, including a former CIA official.
After the countries said in a statement that the conference programme “didn’t align with their official views on the US role in disinformation,” a series of logos – including those of the Lithuanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the European External Action Service (EEAS) and Global Affairs Canada, the Canadian Ministry of Foreign Affairs – were taken down from the event website.
The logos were removed from the event’s signage at such short notice that organisers had no time to replace it and had to improvise a quick fix, with official conference materials being left bearing white stickers covering the logos of the departing sponsors, as photos circulating online show.
Lithuania, Canada, and EEAS pulled out of #Disinfo2026 at such short notice they didn't have time to redo the signage.
— @eliothiggins.bsky.social (@eliothiggins.bsky.social.bsky.social) 2026-10-09T14:03:51.262Z
Supporting independent research
However, Surfshark’s logo remained visible. The VPN provider said that independent research and open debate are essential to its mission of protecting people’s digital lives. “We will continue supporting the communities working to keep the internet open and secure,” it said.
During the event, the VPN presented research carried out in collaboration with students from Malmö University. The study revealed that over half of those surveyed are unable to identify bots or distinguish between social media accounts generated by AI and those managed by real people, leaving them vulnerable to digital threats. It also highlighted how false content contributes to creating a climate of mistrust, disinformation and hostile and malicious online environments.
Recent research by Surfshark also found that more than 6.3 billion fake accounts are removed from major social media platforms annually, and AI only exacerbates the problem, facilitating scams involving identity theft, fraudulent calls, financial fraud and disinformation spreading.
In this context, Surfshark emphasised that fostering open debate remains crucial for raising public awareness of these issues, regardless of diplomatic complexities. “We believe that independent forums examining digital threats must continue to exist – regardless of geopolitical sensitivities – because cybersecurity concerns everyone, and digital risks know no borders,” the VPN said.
Silvia Iacovcich is a tech journalist with over five years of experience in the field, including AI, cybersecurity, and fintech. She has written for various publications focusing on the evolving regulatory landscape of AI, digital behavior, web3, and blockchain, as well as social media privacy and security regulations.

articles.title: AMD tried to crush the 'megahertz myth' 25 years ago today, debuting its Performance Rating system
articles.text:
AMD tried to crush the 'megahertz myth' 25 years ago today, debuting its Performance Rating system — Athlon XP chips introduced the scheme, which endured until Intel lost its clock advantage, focus shifted to multi-core
The relatively short-lived naming convention was thought by some to be a ‘Pentium Rating.’
A quarter century ago today, AMD launched its AMD Athlon XP processor family. These were highly performant processors based on the firm’s latest Palomino core, but ran at lower raw clock speeds than Intel rivals. Facing a marketing imbalance between perceived and actual performance, AMD mounted a serious campaign to explode the 'megahertz myth' with this generation of CPUs. Thus, it introduced new Athlon XP processors with a Performance Rating (PR) designation, alongside a slogan insisting “Performance matters more than MHz.”
Intel, with its Pentium 4 processors, was clearly winning the MHz race at the time, while a CPU’s clock speed had long been established by marketers as a key performance metric. Unfortunately for AMD, its CPUs of the era didn’t hit such high clocks, even though the application and gaming performance was just as good (if not better) than Intel's.
Thomas Pabst's view
Our tests from October 2001 noted that AMD wisely undersold its chips, using the newly devised PR naming system. Anything less and it would have faced strong opposition and derision. Our tests clearly showed that a new “AthlonXP 1800+ is able to beat Intel's flagship Pentium 4 2 GHz in the majority of benchmarks,” wrote the original Tom, Thomas Pabst, in a 13-page feature about AMD’s newest CPUs. Moreover, it was observed that “AthlonXP at 1533 MHz is able to reach or even beat Pentium 4 running at an almost 33% higher clock speed.” Pabst concluded that AMD’s clocks/performance situation forced this concerted stand against the MHz myth.
As we broke the news about AMD’s Performance Rating system, some almost straight-away alluded to it being a ‘Pentium Rating’ system, but it was very early days. We didn’t know whether it would become a long-term success. It was known that AMD planned to establish an independent institution to create a new performance measure that is fairer and more realistic than the current MHz system in the following year. But, of course, Intel wouldn’t be interested in validating that. Pabst concluded that “I might not like it too much,” but admitted AMD had little alternative marketing-wise in the Pentium vs. Athlon era at the beginning of the millennium.
Please stop, it hertz
The AMD PR system would be abandoned roughly five years after it was initiated. Subsequent AMD (and Intel) architectures stopped the rating from making practical sense as the market evolved. For example, Intel’s big MHz advantage was lost in the transition from Pentium 4 Netburst to Pentium M/Core chips. Then, the Athlon 64 was so well received by reviewers and enthusiasts that AMD probably felt it might be wise to finish with its inferiority complex PR system that tied it to its obvious rival. Lastly, by the end of the AMD PR era, the marketing fight was clearly going multi-core. CPU marketing and naming completely sidelined any hint at CPU clock speeds later in the noughties.

Mark Tyson is a news editor at Tom's Hardware. He enjoys covering the full breadth of PC tech; from business and semiconductor design to products approaching the edge of reason.

So, the perception was that AMD performance was waning, when in fact they were doing a decent job of competing....
Later, the bulldozer architecture would find them trailing Intel's CoreDuo architecture by every measurable degree for some time.
It wasn't until the Zen architecture arrived that we saw AMD being truly competitive on a clock and IPC basis with Intel and it's Core architecture (I think they got rid of the 2Duo part of the name). Reply

Bulldozer was awful, but a valuable lesson for AMD. Just throwing more cores on a chip doesn't cut it, they have to communicate better. Thus Zen was born. Reply

articles.title: ¿Multas de 200 euros por no llevar un nuevo bote obligatorio en el maletero desde el 1 de octubre? No tan rápido
articles.text:
Mucho se ha escrito sobre el cambio de normativa del 1 de octubre. Desde hace poco más de una semana, los conductores, motoristas, usuarios de patinetes y/o ciclistas nos enfrentamos a algunos cambios que tratan de mejorar la seguridad de los usuarios más vulnerables. Eso nos ha llevado a leer multitud de informaciones. En Xataka hemos tratado de desgranarlas todas.
Pero como (casi) siempre cuando entra en vigor un cambio normativo en Tráfico, también se han desatado los bulos. O informaciones que los bordean.
¿Qué ha pasado? Como te contamos en Xataka, el pasado verano el Gobierno aprobó una serie de medidas a aplicar a partir del 1 de octubre. Esas nuevas exigencias en la conducción modifican el Reglamento General de Circulación con el objetivo, según el Gobierno, de proteger a los usuarios vulnerables.
Los cambios afectan a todos los usuarios de la vía pero en un resumen rápido te contamos los más sustanciales:
- Los motoristas tendrán que contar con guantes y calzado cerrado
- Los motoristas podrán utilizar el arcén (pero tendrá que estar señalizado en la carretera)
- Antes de adelantar a un ciclista tendremos que reducir la velocidad a, como mínimo, 20 km/h por debajo de la velocidad máxima permitida en la vía
- Los ciclistas podrán circular a contramarcha en calles de un solo carril y sentido (pero tendrá que estar señalizado en la calle)
- Los peatones tendrán preferencia en las vías donde calzada y acera están sobre la misma plataforma
Bordeando el bulo. Estos cambios han propiciado que la red se llene de informaciones sobre lo que cambia a partir del 1 de octubre. En los medios se han analizado los cambios uno por uno, explicando qué hay que tener en cuenta desde este mes.
Pero también se han multiplicado las informaciones sobre supuestas nuevas normas aplicadas desde el 1 de octubre que son mentira. O, al menos, es mentira que haya cambiado algo desde hace poco más de una semana. En esas informaciones se ha intentado meter en la coctelera la fecha en cuestión y elementos polémicos como la baliza V-16 para generar visitas.
Nada nuevo. Una de las informaciones que se ha viralizado es que desde el 1 de octubre se está castigando con 200 euros a quienes no lleven un bote obligatorio en el maletero pese a que sí lleven la baliza V-16.
Ese "bote obligatorio" es, en realidad, el kit reparapinchazos (o una rueda de repuesto en su lugar). Esto era ya obligatorio antes del 1 de octubre, por lo que no hay nada nuevo por aquí.
Además, hay que recalcar que no llevar el kit reparapinchazos o la rueda de repuesto está recogido como una infracción leve en la Ley de Tráfico, tal y como nos ha confirmado la DGT. Por tanto, la sanción de no tener disponibles una de estas opciones en el coche es de 80 euros.
Y la baliza V-16. Efectivamente, el nuevo cambio en el reglamento tampoco supone ninguna modificación en la obligación de llevar la baliza V-16 y cómo utilizarla. Es obligatorio contar con este dispositivo en el coche y no hacerlo puede conllevar una multa de 80 euros, la misma que se aplicaba por no contar con los triángulos en el coche.
Así mismo, en caso de avería o accidente leve, sigue siendo obligatorio activar la baliza y situarla en el techo del coche antes de salir del vehículo. Además, sólo está permitido salir del mismo con chaleco reflectante y siempre y cuando exista un lugar que nos permita esperar a los servicios de auxilio desde un espacio lo suficientemente seguro.

articles.title: Weniger Admin, mehr Entscheidung: Was KI-Agenten für KMU leisten können
articles.text:
Weniger Admin, mehr Entscheidung: Was KI-Agenten für KMU leisten können
Warum KI-Agenten für KMU jetzt relevant werden
Der Mittelstand steht unter Druck: knappe Ressourcen, komplexere Lieferketten, mehr Dokumentationspflichten und steigende Erwartungen an Geschwindigkeit. Genau hier können KI-Agenten ansetzen. Sie übernehmen nicht einfach einzelne Textaufgaben, sondern können Informationen bündeln, Daten prüfen und Arbeitsschritte beschleunigen.
Eine aktuelle YouGov-Umfrage im Auftrag von Alibaba.com und dem Bundesverband E-Commerce und Versandhandel (bevh) zeigt: Rund ein Drittel der KMU sieht administrative Überlastung als konkretes Problem. Rund 40 Prozent nennen Auftragsabwicklung und Kundenservice als besonders zeitintensive Bereiche. Mehr als die Hälfte der KMU ab zehn Mitarbeitern sieht zudem das Potenzial, durch KI-Agenten mindestens zehn Prozent operativer Routineaufgaben einzusparen.
Vom Admin-Overload zu mehr Entscheidungsstärke
Der größte Hebel liegt dort, wo Unternehmen heute besonders viel Zeit verlieren: in fragmentierten Informationen, wiederkehrenden Prüfungen und manuellen Abstimmungen. KI-Agenten können Daten aus verschiedenen Quellen zusammenführen, Dokumente vorstrukturieren, Kriterien abgleichen und nächste Schritte vorbereiten oder ausführen.
Das entlastet Teams im Tagesgeschäft und schafft bessere Grundlagen für Entscheidungen. Besonders relevant ist das in Bereichen wie Auftragsabwicklung, Kundenservice, Compliance, Produktrecherche, Angebotsvorbereitung und internationaler Beschaffung.
Jüngere Entscheider treiben die Nutzung voran
Besonders dynamisch ist die Entwicklung bei jüngeren Führungskräften. In der Gruppe der unter 35-Jährigen nutzen mehr als 62 Prozent bereits Agentic AI. Gleichzeitig investiert in dieser Altersgruppe fast jeder Vierte gezielt in KI-Weiterbildung und ein Drittel sieht ohne KI-Agenten mittelfristig Risiken für die eigene Wettbewerbsfähigkeit. Auch beim Vertrauen in KI-gestützte Ergebnisse liegen jüngere Entscheider klar vorn, etwa bei der Prüfung von Produktinformationen, Lieferantenangaben oder der Vorbereitung von Geschäftsdokumenten. Die Entwicklung ist damit weniger ein Hinweis auf Zurückhaltung im Mittelstand als vielmehr ein positives Signal: Eine neue Generation von Entscheidern zeigt, wie schnell KI-Agenten vom Experiment zum produktiven Werkzeug werden können.
Accio: Agentische KI für den B2B-Alltag
Accio zeigt, wie dieser Wandel praktisch aussehen kann. Die Agentic AI-Plattform unterstützt Unternehmen dabei, Produktideen zu entwickeln, Markt- und Trenddaten zu analysieren, Lieferanteninformationen zu vergleichen, Spezifikationen und Zertifikate schneller einzuordnen und Geschäftsprozesse von Anfang bis Ende zu automatisieren.
Damit adressiert Accio zentrale Engpässe im B2B-Alltag: Recherche, Datenabgleich, Dokumentenprüfung, Angebotsvorbereitung und Beschaffungsentscheidungen. Unternehmen gewinnen Zeit, reduzieren Routineaufwand und können sich stärker auf Bewertung, Strategie und Wachstum konzentrieren.
Alibaba.com lädt Unternehmer aus Deutschland und ganz Europa ein, diese technologischen Möglichkeiten durch den CoCreate Pitch Europe in die Praxis umzusetzen. Der Startup-Wettbewerb unterstützt kleine Unternehmen dabei, den nächsten Schritt in der KI-Nutzung zu gehen. In diesem Jahr werden alle Bewerbungen über Accio eingereicht, von der Marktforschung über Produktideen bis hin zur Bewertung geschäftlicher Chancen. Die europäischen Finalrunden finden am 19. und 20. November in London statt. Weitere Informationen finden Sie auf der Event-Seite zum CoCreate Pitch.
Fazit: Die Chance liegt im Jetzt
Für den Mittelstand liegt die Chance nicht in einem radikalen Bruch, sondern in einem pragmatischen Produktivitätsschub. Wachstumsstarke KMU und jüngere Entscheider machen bereits vor, wie KI-Agenten operative Arbeit erleichtern können. Wer jetzt erste Anwendungsfelder identifiziert, kann Effizienzpotenziale heben, bevor aus Vorsprung Nachholbedarf wird.

articles.title: The director of Fjord takes the ‘risky position’ of moderator
articles.text:
Cristian Mungiu’s sixth feature, Fjord, concerns a family on trial. They seem like good people, God-fearing. They’ve just moved from Romania to a small hamlet nestled in the fjords of rural Norway. There is Mamma (Renate Reinsve), Tata (a bald and bespectacled Sebastian Stan), and their passel of children. They are an openly religious and proselytizing family. The parents, unfashionably, believe in punitive consequences to actions. They would never be accused of gentle parenting. All ought to be well, only Norway in 2026 is extravagantly suspicious of the devout — their famous tolerance reserved for the secular.
The director of Fjord takes the ‘risky position’ of moderator
With his new film about a Romanian family’s life in Norway, Cristian Mungiu wants you to consider the limits of your tolerance
Fjord starts quietly and builds subtly. We are with the family as they are introduced to their places of learning, employment, and worship. A second, Norwegian, family serves as their foil. Sort of. Questions arise, about what counts as discipline, what as punishment. To those wanting answers, objective analysis, which is to say a kind of measured purity, Mungiu says, come down to the mud with us! In the morally complex world of the movie, nothing is spared — a piano chord, a passing remark, hems of clothes — all are cast in a different light. We are all the more enriched for it.
The Verge spoke with Mungiu, who is himself Romanian, about how his early tenure in journalism informs his writing, what it was like living under Nicolae Ceaușescu’s dictatorial reign, Marxist literary theory, and the challenges and pleasures of thinking for oneself.
This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.
I’d like to start with you at Cannes, where you said the question that Fjord raises is: Are there good minorities and bad minorities? I wonder if this question has changed for you since.
Not so much. I think that as much as we need to understand that there are good values in society, like tolerance for all the other minorities and inclusion of those who are different than us, we should always focus on this idea that sometimes even if there are minorities with whom we don’t share the same values, we need to be tolerant to those as well. If not, what makes us believe that we have a more liberal, progressive view on the world?
Of course, there is a limit. We all need to condemn violence, and we all need to be on the same side of helping people out.
But whenever we talk about, for example, religious beliefs, even if we are people who don’t share such beliefs, it’s good to be tolerant with them, if they want to share different views. You need to let them be.
“Even if there are minorities with whom we don’t share the same values, we need to be tolerant to those as well.”
There are so many people next to us who share a lot of irrational beliefs, from reading the horoscope to believing in alternative medicine. We let them be. Why would we condemn people for being religious? It’s good to try to convince them that actually it’s good to see that your beliefs are based on something rational, because eventually, we all influence the lives of others, and it’s good to make choices based on rational things. But you need to advance little by little, step by step. I don’t believe in this way of imposing views on others and making rules for others to change what they think. If you do that, you will only radicalize people.
You said you kept chancing upon articles about immigrant families in Nordic countries. Is reading the news part of your practice? Otherwise, where have your ideas come from?
I read a lot of news every day, and I keep a lot of these articles in special folders under different themes. And it took years before I decided to make a film based on the ideas in these articles, because in the beginning they are very spectacular. They are just informing us about something spectacular that has happened. While for me, the film should be something deeper, more profound, in the sense that I’m trying to figure out why those things have happened and what do they tell us about the world around us?
I try to avoid the sensational part of it and to try to dig down, and to understand what is it that it could tell you about your own life, and this is what I did for the original story as well. I needed some eight years from the moment when I read about it to the moment when I decided to make a film out of it.
Tell me more about your excavation process. Can you walk us through what is actually happening in those eight years? And specifically, can you tell us about the moment in the process when you go from research to fiction? What does that leap look like, or maybe it’s seamless?
It’s fair to say that I haven’t used all these 10 years to investigate. But I was aware all the time that this exists. For example, I decided to talk to this family who was involved in the most prominent case, in the most spoken-about case, from three years ago. I talked to them. I talked to their children. I went to Norway. I met their relatives. I went to see the house where everything happened. I took advantage in that moment to investigate more, and I met everybody that I could who was involved in that case. And people who were willing to talk to me. I talked to lawyers. I talked to all the press that covered the case. I talked to the translator they were having when talking to the police. I talked to the Barnevernet [Norwegian child welfare agency]. I talked to the NGOs who were involved a lot in such cases. Later on, I was a witness to the trials they were having on children issues. So I did my best to find all the points of view of people involved, not only in that case but in other cases.
And finally, I crafted the screenplay based a lot on the arguments that I was recording. I didn’t have to invent much. I just needed to organize the material, but I didn’t need to build a lot on what are the arguments of each of these two sides.
The fictional part of the film comes a lot from this second family, which is fully fictional, and that gave me the possibility of following the film from the point of view of the adults. I needed to be with the family, but I wanted to balance this point of view of the family with the point of view of another family with children and sharing the values of the society in which they live, a family with whom they need to communicate with because they are secluded in this fjord at the end of the world, and it was important for me to see how these values collide, and what changes in this process of being forced to communicate with others.
Tell us about your time as a reporter, early in your career. How did you decide to turn to film?
I started working in the press in 1987, and also this was a part of me getting closer to what I wanted to do. I wished that I could become a storyteller, and I wished already at that age — I was 19 — that I could become a filmmaker. Back then, becoming a student at the film school during communist times wasn’t really a fair process, so it wasn’t for me. So I was starting to get closer to becoming a writer. This is what I thought I could do. I started writing. And then I got to this newspaper, and I started practicing my writing and taking pictures. Two activities which were as close as I could to becoming a filmmaker without being able to become one on the spot. A lot of my style of writing screenplays today is still based on that period in which I learned how to write a piece of news.
But happily, you know, the wall fell. Communism collapsed. It was very passionate to be in the press for a while because people were hungry for what they were calling “truth” after such a long period in which we didn’t have a free press.
My style of writing was shaped in that period. I am not bringing, when I describe things, my own point of view. I’m describing an external situation, the way in which these things manifest, but I don’t draw the conclusion. I depict a situation, and I encourage you to use your critical spirit to understand the way it manifests. I am encouraging you also to take on this responsibility as a spectator, in which I’m not guiding you through the story. You have your freedom of interpreting based on facts, and making sure you analyze the facts. If you’re just analyzing what the characters say, you might be very easily manipulated. Manipulated, because, as you know, in cinema, characters lie, and are as manipulative as people are in real lives.
So it’s not that you wanted to be a filmmaker as such, but that you wanted to be a storyteller, and you found film?
I wanted to be a storyteller, and I thought that I’m going to be a writer. Then I was undergoing this period in my life in which I was watching a lot of films, very popular films.
Also being influenced by the Romanian films that I could watch in the period, which were very strange. Maybe it was, in part, the censorship, but probably it was also that the people that were encouraged to make films were not very talented. But they seemed to be made with people looking like us, and apparently using the same language as us, but actually nothing like that ever happened in reality. They were psychologically so unbelievable, and the dialogue was also a message that somebody wrote in the right order grammatically, and it was pure propaganda.
So, we started developing this idea that it shouldn’t be this complicated to make films. You just need to co-opt reality.
I want to tell you something funny about the message that I got today. Following a lot of these cases in the Nordic countries and talking to so many people, I became some sort of an expert.
I got a message this morning from a half-German, half-Norwegian family saying, Help. Help us. Nothing has changed. I’m trying to bring this forward. This is a topic about which we all need to have an opinion. But I’m not this superhero that can solve the situation.
It’s important to make this clear that the film is not just about Romania and Norway and the Barnevernet. The film is about what happens in the States too, for example. I think that this polarization of people needs to have an answer because we can’t continue living in these bubbles. This degree of hatred and aggression, which might end up badly, and very violent.
What do you do when people call you for help?
They text, and I’m answering back.
I started this promotional tour in Norway, and I met a lot of people from both sides talking to me. We ran across this very difficult confession of a spectator, this lady who was crying, telling us that she was experiencing these cases with such emotion that finally she decided, for fear of having her children taken away by the authorities, she decided to rather have an abortion.
We also met people telling us that they are 100 percent behind the point of view of the protection in the film, because if they were in the situation of having their children taken in a conservative society, nobody would care for them. I think this shows that people rather tend to imagine that the wrong and radical way of seeing the society can be compensated by another wrong and radical way, and this shouldn’t be the answer. The answer should be more attempts at integration, trying to be more empathic and more open to dialogue, if we wish to give a good example to the part of the society who think they can’t escape this idea that they already know the truth and there’s no way out.
In the court scene, Sebastian Stan’s character gestures at the ways in which liberal societies privilege physical harm over emotional or verbal harm. There is, of course, no such thing as a view from nowhere. I know you said your opinion doesn’t matter, but I would still like to know how you relate or do not relate to this argument.
Of course, we need to make this clear. As soon as there is proven violence in a family, we all need to act as soon as we can and save them. Be it children or women. Of course, we need to act.
But the film talks about the fact that in most cases, you are supposed to make a choice, not knowing what happened in the family. You are just having assumptions in most of these cases, and this is why Fjord is crafted as such.
After investigating for two years and talking to all the parties involved, I can’t tell if this real family, which was involved in the real case, was violent or not. I don’t know. I’m not saying that they were not. I don’t know, because even if I talk to them and to their children... But I noticed that when people are making choices in Norway, for example, or us in society in general, we tend to be biased by our own stereotypes about the situation, and it’s very difficult to position yourself in an objective point of view. This doesn’t really exist.
“I was curious enough to see what happens in liberal, progressive societies when the conservatives all of a sudden become a minority. ”
So you need to be aware that you’re biased, that you are seeing the situation from your perspective, and when you’re mentioning that you’re doing whatever is best for the benefit of the children, actually you tend to believe that your solution is for the best, while the others will believe the same if they act on their opinions.
And of course, you know, we need to make sure that there is enough freedom accepted by everybody into our societies, so that minorities have the right to be who they want to be.
But after making a film that was speaking a lot about how minorities are being discriminated in conservative society, I was curious enough to see what happens in liberal, progressive societies when the conservatives all of a sudden become a minority. Wouldn’t you expect that they are treated with more empathy for not sharing the same values with the majority? Well, actually, they are not. The fact that you belong to the majority tends to be more important to you than the values that belong to your ideology.
Literary theorist Terry Eagleton has a quote that goes, “Ideology is like bad breath. We only recognize it in other people.”
I understand precise choreography is part of your process. You have talked about how you also try your best to avoid cutting because that is an interpretation. Does that mean the point of art is verisimilitude, capturing reality? And if not that, what are movies for? Why do you make movies?
I believe in diversity in filmmaking, and I think that making entertainment is also a valid way of making films, but it shouldn’t be the only way. The films that I try to make are films that try to make people think a little bit more, and to make them aware of the world which exists next to theirs. I’m using this as a tool to make you aware that you should be very careful of what happens next to you.
There isn’t anything like an objective point of view, but the best I could do is not to be manipulative with my style. I’m not making a film biased by one of these points of view. I’m taking this risky position of a moderator, bringing two sets of values in front of you so that you can double check your values and to remember when was the last time when you doubted that you are on the good side of things? Everybody else is so convinced that they are as right as you, but you know the first step into entering some sort of a dialogue is listening to others.
Fjord was released in select US theaters October 9th, with a wide release on October 23rd.

articles.title: US bars Microsoft, Indian IT firms from green card programme; TCS Q2 net profit rises 15%
articles.text:
US bars Microsoft, Indian IT firms from green card programme; TCS Q2 net profit rises 15%
The United States government is suspending new applications for permanent residency of foreign workers at companies including Microsoft, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, and HCLTech, citing abuse in the entire process.
Dear Reader,
The United States government is suspending new applications for permanent residency of foreign workers at companies including Microsoft, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, and HCLTech, citing abuse in the entire process.
In a particular reference to Microsoft, US Vice President J D Vance said, “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.”
In other news, Prime Minister Narendra Modi has called for a global framework to tackle cyber frauds and deepfakes. At the tenth edition of the India Mobile Congress, PM Modi said governments, technology companies, telecom operators, and financial institutions should create mechanisms to curb digital frauds.
Meanwhile, India aims to double its 5G user base from 550 million to 1 billion by 2030, and up its game with 6G. Though the country had been behind in 4G, it marched with the world in 5G, and is now determined to take the lead in 6G, said Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia said, at the mobile congress.
In funding news, DailyObjects, a design-led lifestyle-tech brand, has raised Rs 332 crore in a Series C round of funding led by Xponentia Capital Partners, Anicut Capital, and Axiom Asia Private Capital.
There’s a lot of chatter around founder burnout and stress. But a new study points out that startup employees may need greater attention.
Nearly half (47.5%) of people working in India’s startup ecosystem report low wellbeing, with employees faring the worst, according to a ‘State of Mind: The Startup Ecosystem’ study. The survey found that 54.3% of employees scored at or below the wellbeing threshold, compared with 45.2% of investors, 44.2% of ecosystem supporters, and 42.9% of founders.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- TCS Q2 net profit rises 15%
- Women’s ride safety: Not just another feature on the app
Here’s your trivia for today: What device was the first Sony-branded product, released in 1955? (Scroll down for the answer)
Corporate
TCS Q2 net profit rises 15%
Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), India’s largest IT services exporter, registered a 15% rise in net profit and an 11.2% growth in revenue for the second quarter of the fiscal. Its performance was in line with market expectations.
The company attributed this performance to its international growth and certain deal wins during the quarter. It also noted that its annualised revenues from artificial intelligence (AI) has exceeded $3 billion.
Key takeaways:
- TCS has reported a net profit of Rs 13,884 crore for the July to September period of FY27, against Rs 12,075 crore in the similar period a year ago. Revenue was Rs 73,188 crore, compared to Rs 65,799 crore a year ago.
- TCS CEO K Krithivasan said, “We are pleased with the broad-based growth in all our international markets and most industry segments. This quarter we announced two unique deals with Porsche and Best Buy which represent a new category of transformation partnerships. Together with our clients, we are building repeatable value platforms that will industrialise AI at scale.”
- The manufacturing and energy & utilities segments posted strong growth for TCS. The BFSI segment is showing signs of revival. In terms of geography, TCS’ growth came from the UK and Continental Europe, while the North America region posted a modest rise.
Insight
Women’s ride safety cannot be just another feature on the app
There are several crucial questions when it comes to the safety of women passengers using app-based rides. Should the responsibility for staying safe always begin and end with the woman in the back seat? What responsibility should the mobility system itself bear for keeping women safe?
The National Commission for Women’s (NCW) new guidelines for the safety of women passengers using digital transport services seek to make women’s safety a shared responsibility of platforms, authorities, and law enforcement.
Key takeaways:
- The NCW guidelines aim to strengthen preventive safeguards, improve coordination between key stakeholders, and establish stronger response mechanisms at different stages of a woman’s journey.
- The real test lies in implementation. Coordination will matter as much as the technology. A route-deviation alert is useful only if someone responds immediately. An SOS button matters only if a functioning response system backs it up. A complaint mechanism means little if a woman still has to repeatedly explain what happened.
- For women, safer mobility is about being able to travel with confidence when the systems designed to protect them work when they need them.
News & updates
- Govt responds to Musk: The government has condemned Elon Musk over his allegations that Starlink’s satcom services are being blocked. It has also clarified that every satcom licensee in the country must comply with security norms. The statement comes after Musk alleged that “certain oligarchs” have blocked his company’s satellite communication services in India to maintain their monopoly in the country.
- Content crackdown: Meta said it has deployed new AI tools to crack down on ads that covertly lead users to child abuse material, as it disclosed that it acted on 5.3 million pieces of child sexual exploitation content in India during the first half of 2026.
- Record quarter: TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, reported a record third-quarter revenue of $46.71 billion, beating market forecasts and rising 50% from the year-earlier period due to surging demand for AI applications.
